📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — classify the computer from the clues

WORKED EXAMPLE — match machine to class
• “Runs climate simulations, measured in petaFLOPS” → supercomputer (raw floating-point throughput).
• “Serves millions of web requests in a data center” → server / warehouse-scale computer (throughput + availability).
• “A phone: battery-limited, tightly integrated SoC” → personal mobile device (energy efficiency dominates).
• “A chip inside an insulin pump running one fixed program” → embedded computer (cost/power/fixed function).
The tell is the DESIGN GOAL: FLOPS → super, throughput → server, energy → mobile, cost+fixed-function → embedded. Different classes optimize different metrics — that’s the exam’s recurring question.
⚠️ EMBEDDED IS THE BIGGEST CLASS
By unit count, embedded processors dwarf PCs and servers combined — most computers you own you never see. “Most common class of computer” = embedded.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Computer architecture isn't one thing — it's a family of designs optimized for very different uses. A smartphone, a laptop, a server, a supercomputer, and a microcontroller all run code, but the constraints driving each design diverge sharply. Knowing the classes helps you read any architecture decision in context.

Core concepts

1. Personal Mobile Devices (PMDs). Phones, tablets, smartwatches. Battery-powered, so energy efficiency dominates. ARM processors are universal here. Real-time responsiveness matters (touch latency); raw throughput less so. Modern PMDs are powerful enough that the line with laptops blurs.

2. Desktops and laptops. General-purpose, plugged in or with substantial battery. Balance performance, energy, and cost. x86 (Intel/AMD) historically dominant; ARM (Apple Silicon) increasingly competitive. Workloads vary widely — anything from web browsing to compilation to gaming.

3. Servers. Run continuously in data centers. Optimize for throughput per watt and reliability over latency. Multiple sockets common; large memory; redundant power and cooling. Workloads: web serving, databases, virtualization, batch processing. Most cloud computing happens on these.

4. Supercomputers. The largest end. Thousands to millions of cores in coordination. Optimize for sustained floating-point throughput on parallelizable workloads (climate modeling, molecular dynamics, training large AI models). Cost in millions to billions; ranked by FLOPS on the TOP500 list.

5. Embedded systems. Microcontrollers and processors built into other things — cars, appliances, industrial controllers, IoT devices. Hard real-time constraints (anti-lock braking can't miss a deadline). Tight memory, often no OS or a real-time OS. Hidden but vastly outnumber the visible computers.

6. Cloud computing. Not a class of hardware exactly — a model of delivery. Servers in data centers rented by virtual machine, container, or function. Hides the hardware behind APIs. Most modern application workloads run on cloud servers; few teams operate physical infrastructure anymore.

7. The post-PC era. Sales of PMDs dwarf desktops. Most users access computing through phones, tablets, and cloud services. PC sales remain meaningful but no longer drive the market. Architecture decisions optimize for mobile and server first; desktop second.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Assuming server hardware design carries over to embedded — they have opposite priorities.
  • Treating cloud as 'just servers' — its API/abstraction layer changes economics and architecture practice.
  • Underestimating embedded systems — they're the largest category by unit count, and getting them wrong has physical consequences.
  • Thinking smartphone design has no architectural influence on servers — Apple's ARM-based Mac transition shows how PMD energy techniques flow upward.

Quick recap

Computers come in classes optimized for distinct uses: PMDs prioritize energy and responsiveness; desktops/laptops balance broadly; servers maximize throughput per watt; supercomputers maximize floating-point on parallel workloads; embedded systems meet real-time deadlines on tight resources. Cloud is a delivery model layered on servers. The post-PC era shifted volume to mobile and cloud.

Glossary

PMD (Personal Mobile Device)
Battery-powered handheld or wearable computer; phones, tablets, watches.
SMP (Symmetric Multi-Processor)
Architecture with multiple identical processors sharing memory.
Embedded system
Computer built into another device for a dedicated purpose.
Cloud computing
Model of delivering computing as a service over the network from data centers.
Post-PC era
Period when smartphone and tablet sales surpassed traditional PC sales as the dominant computing form factor.

Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the steps, in order
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

A computer is a stack of abstractions. A single click triggers software, which talks to an operating system, which executes machine instructions, which run on circuits, which are built from transistors and atoms. No engineer holds all of it in their head simultaneously — each layer hides the messiness beneath it. Understanding this hierarchy lets you (1) debug at the right level when things break, (2) know when to drop down a layer for speed or memory wins, and (3) reason about performance, security, and reliability across the whole stack. Computer architecture (C952) sits in the middle of this stack — above the physics, below the operating system — and everything you learn here clicks into context once you see the layers.

The classic abstraction stack

From bottom (physics) to top (your app), the canonical layers:

LayerWhat it deals withWho works here
ApplicationSolves a user problem (browser, game, IDE)App developers
High-level languagePython, Java, C++ — readable code with variables, loops, classesAll programmers
Compiler / interpreterTranslates HLL → assembly / bytecode / machine codeCompiler engineers
AssemblyHuman-readable instruction mnemonics (ADD, LW, BEQ)Systems programmers
Operating systemManages CPU time, memory, files, devices, networkingOS engineers
Instruction Set Architecture (ISA)The contract: what instructions the CPU promises to runArchitects (RISC-V, ARM, x86)
MicroarchitectureHOW the CPU implements the ISA (pipelining, caches, branch prediction)CPU designers
Digital logicAND/OR/NOT gates, flip-flops, multiplexersLogic designers
Transistors / circuitsCMOS, voltages, switching, current flowVLSI / EE
PhysicsSemiconductors, electron behavior, quantum effects at small scalesPhysicists / device engineers

Each layer EXPOSES a clean interface to the layer above, and HIDES the complexity below. That's the definition of an abstraction.

What "abstraction" really buys you

An abstraction is a contract — a promise of WHAT happens without specifying HOW. The ISA is the most studied example in C952:

  • Promise (interface): "If you write the instruction ADD x1, x2, x3, the value in register x1 will become the sum of x2 and x3 by the next clock cycle."
  • Hidden (implementation): Inside the CPU, that ADD might be pipelined across 5 stages, forwarded through bypass paths, speculatively executed before its inputs are even known, then committed in-order. None of that matters to the programmer — only the contract matters.

This separation is what lets a program compiled in 1995 still run on a 2026 CPU. The ISA hasn't changed (much). The microarchitecture beneath has been re-engineered a dozen times.

★ THE ISA-MICROARCH SPLIT IS THE KEY

The Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) is the visible contract. The microarchitecture is the hidden implementation. Two CPUs can share an ISA (both run RISC-V code) but have wildly different microarchitectures (one cheap and slow, one expensive and fast). C952 spends most of its time on the ISA layer because that's the layer programmers and compilers see directly.

Why layers exist: managing complexity

A modern Intel CPU has billions of transistors. No human team could design billions of transistors from scratch. Instead:

  1. Transistor engineers design ~50 standard cells (NAND, NOR, flip-flop, MUX).
  2. Logic designers compose those cells into adders, multipliers, register files.
  3. Microarchitects compose those blocks into pipelines, caches, branch predictors.
  4. Architects define the ISA so the compiler and OS know what's promised.
  5. OS engineers build kernels assuming the ISA holds.
  6. Compiler engineers translate Python/Java to that ISA.
  7. App devs write Python, never thinking about voltages.

Without this layered division of labor, modern computing wouldn't exist.

Leaky abstractions

"All abstractions leak" — Joel Spolsky, 2002. The abstraction breaks down, and you suddenly have to know about the layer below.

Examples:

  • Garbage collection: Hides memory management... until your Java app pauses for 2 seconds during a GC sweep and you have to learn about generational collectors.
  • Virtual memory: Hides physical memory location... until your laptop swaps to disk and your game stutters because the OS evicted a needed page.
  • HTTP libraries: Hide TCP/IP... until you see a connection reset and need to debug raw packets.
  • SQL: Hides storage and indexes... until a query takes 30 minutes and you have to read query plans.
  • Compilers: Hide assembly... until you optimize a hot loop and need to look at the generated code.

The abstraction stack is the BEST tool we have for managing complexity, but it's never perfect. A good engineer knows when to drop down a level.

Hardware vs software boundary

Where exactly is the line between "hardware" and "software"? It depends who you ask:

  • App programmer: The OS is "below me, basically hardware."
  • OS programmer: The ISA is "below me, basically hardware."
  • Microarchitect: The transistor library is "below me, basically physics."
  • EE: The semiconductor wafer is "below me, basically physics."

The honest answer: there isn't ONE line. Each layer is hardware to the layer above and software to the layer below (the chip designer writes "Verilog" — software that describes hardware).

Performance from understanding the stack

Why does any of this matter for performance? Because the LAYER WHERE YOU FIX A PROBLEM determines the COST and the SPEEDUP:

Where you fix itSpeedup possibleCost
Better algorithm (HLL)10×–1000×Days
Better data structure2×–100×Days
Compiler optimization flags1.5×–3×Hours
Hand-tuned assembly (rare)1.5×–5× on hot loopsWeeks
Cache-friendly memory layout2×–20×Days–weeks
Custom hardware (FPGA, ASIC)100×–1000×Months–years

Lesson: ALWAYS start at the top of the stack (algorithm) and only drop down when you've exhausted the easier wins.

RISC-V — a clean example

C952 uses RISC-V because it shows the abstraction stack with minimal mess:

  • ISA layer: ~50 base integer instructions. Clean, regular, well-documented.
  • Microarchitecture: Reference implementations range from tiny embedded cores (4-stage pipeline) to massive server cores (out-of-order, 6-wide issue, large caches).
  • Same ISA, different microarchitectures — every RISC-V chip runs your binary unchanged, but performance varies 1000×.

Contrast with x86: same idea, but the ISA has accumulated 40 years of additions and the microarchitecture inside Intel/AMD CPUs translates x86 to internal "micro-ops" first. The layering is even deeper.

Putting it together

The next time someone says "the computer is slow," ask: at WHICH layer? It might be:

  • Application: bad algorithm, O(n²) where O(n log n) exists
  • OS: process scheduling, swap thrashing
  • ISA / microarch: pipeline stall, cache miss
  • Hardware: thermal throttling, slow SSD

Each requires different debugging tools and different fixes. The whole point of layered abstraction is that you usually only need to know ONE layer well. The whole point of being a CS major is that you've at least PEEKED into every layer so you can find the right one when things break.

✓ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • The computer is a stack: physics → transistors → logic → microarch → ISA → OS → compiler → HLL → app
  • Each layer EXPOSES an interface and HIDES implementation details
  • The ISA is the contract between hardware and software — the most important abstraction in C952
  • Microarchitecture is HOW the ISA gets implemented (pipelining, caches, etc.)
  • All abstractions leak — be ready to drop down a layer when needed
  • Performance fixes scale with which layer you target — algorithm changes give the biggest wins
  • RISC-V is studied because its layers are unusually clean
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — which layer should you fix?

A report generator takes 100 s: 70 s inside an O(n²) sort, 30 s everywhere else. Two engineers propose fixes at different layers. Which wins?

Option A — ALGORITHM layer: replace the O(n^2) sort with O(n log n), 20x faster on this input
  new sort time = 70 / 20            =  3.5 s
  untouched work                     = 30.0 s
  new total = 3.5 + 30.0             = 33.5 s
  speedup   = 100 / 33.5             =  2.99x

Option B — ASSEMBLY layer: hand-tune every hot loop, 1.5x faster overall
  new total = 100 / 1.5              = 66.7 s
  speedup   = 100 / 66.7             =  1.50x

Answer: Option A, 2.99x versus 1.50x — and it takes days instead of weeks.

Read the arithmetic, not the intuition. Option A is a 20x fix but only touches 70% of the time, so Amdahl caps it at 1 / (0.30 + 0.70/20) = 2.99x. Option B is a much weaker fix that touches 100% of the time, and it still loses. The trap is assuming the lowest layer gives the biggest win: dropping to assembly is the hardest work in the stack and usually buys the least. Start at the top of the stack and only descend when the easy wins are gone.

Figure — the stack read as contracts: the ISA row is the one promise hardware makes to software, and everything below that dashed line may change freely.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together

📖 Worked example — from sand to chip, and why yield matters

WORKED EXAMPLE — the manufacturing chain + a yield computation
Silicon ingot → sliced into wafers → patterned into hundreds of dies → tested, cut, packaged into chips.

If a wafer holds 100 dies and 20 have defects, yield = 80/100 = 80%. Cost per GOOD die = wafer cost ÷ good dies: a $4,000 wafer → 4000/80 = $50 per working chip. Bigger dies → fewer per wafer AND more likely to catch a defect → yield falls twice as hard — why huge chips cost disproportionately more.
⚠️ MOORE’S LAW IS ABOUT TRANSISTORS, NOT SPEED
The classic statement: transistor counts per chip double roughly every ~2 years. Clock speeds stopped scaling with them (the power wall) — which is exactly why the industry pivoted to multicore (ch8).
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The advances driving computer architecture are physical — transistors got smaller, cheaper, and faster every couple of years for decades. That trend is breaking down. Knowing where Moore's Law and Dennard scaling came from, and why they're slowing, explains why modern chips are multicore and increasingly specialized.

Core concepts

1. Transistors are the building blocks. A modern CPU has billions of transistors. Each transistor is a tiny switch — billions of them combine into the gates and circuits of a CPU. The shrinking of transistors over decades is what enabled every other architectural improvement.

2. Moore's Law. Gordon Moore (1965): the number of transistors on a chip doubles roughly every two years. Held remarkably well for 50+ years. Result: enormous cost-per-transistor decreases. Slowing now — 3nm, 2nm, but each step harder and more expensive than the last.

3. Dennard scaling — and its end. Robert Dennard (1974): as transistors shrink, voltage and current scale down too, so power density stays constant. Smaller transistors meant faster AND cooler chips. Dennard scaling broke around 2005 — transistors keep shrinking but voltage scaling stalled. Power density rose.

4. The end of frequency scaling. Pre-2005, each chip generation came with higher clock speeds. After Dennard's end, increasing clock speed cooked the chip. Clock speeds have been roughly stable around 3-5 GHz for nearly two decades. The free lunch of 'next year's CPU is just faster' ended.

5. The shift to multicore. Without frequency scaling, manufacturers added more cores instead. Software had to adapt — write parallel code or watch single-thread performance stagnate. The shift is foundational to modern programming. Multicore introduced the parallelism complexity that the rest of the field has been wrestling with for two decades.

6. Specialization and accelerators. When general-purpose performance plateaus, specialize. GPUs for graphics and AI. TPUs for matrix multiplication. NPU for neural networks. FPGA for custom logic. Heterogeneous computing — CPU plus accelerators — is standard in modern systems.

7. Manufacturing and the foundry model. VLSI (Very Large Scale Integration) lithography prints billions of transistors per chip. The leading-edge foundries (TSMC, Samsung, Intel) cost tens of billions to build. Most chip companies don't own foundries — they design and contract manufacturing. The fabless model dominates.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Quoting Moore's Law as if it's still in full force — it's slowing significantly.
  • Treating Dennard's end as recent news — it's been the dominant constraint for nearly 20 years.
  • Expecting next-gen CPUs to be dramatically faster on single-threaded workloads — they aren't.
  • Underestimating manufacturing complexity — leading-edge fabs are among the most complex industrial processes ever built.

Quick recap

Transistors shrank for decades, doubling per Moore's Law every two years, with Dennard scaling keeping power density constant. Dennard scaling ended around 2005; frequency scaling stopped. The industry shifted to multicore, then to specialized accelerators (GPUs, TPUs, NPUs). Leading-edge manufacturing is dominated by a few foundries. The 'free lunch' of free performance per generation is over.

Glossary

Moore's Law
Observation that transistor count per chip doubles roughly every two years.
Dennard scaling
Trend (1974-~2005) of voltage scaling alongside transistor shrink, keeping power density constant.
Multicore
Strategy of adding multiple processor cores to one chip when frequency scaling stopped.
VLSI
Very Large Scale Integration; lithographic process for producing billions of transistors per chip.
Foundry
Semiconductor manufacturing facility; leading-edge ones are operated by a small number of companies (TSMC, Samsung, Intel).

📘 Deep dive: chip yield, binning & cooling

Yield is the percentage of dies on a wafer that work — defects (dust, lithography flaws) kill dies, and larger dies suffer more, which is why yield drops as chips grow. Binning: manufacturers test each working chip and sell it at the speed/core-count it can sustain — one production line yields several product tiers. Faster, denser chips generate more heat, so cooling (heat sinks, fans, liquid) is a first-class design constraint, not an afterthought.

How chips are made: integrated circuits are fabricated on a single silicon wafer by depositing and etching microscopic layers (photolithography) — building up, not carving down. Hundreds of dies are fabricated per wafer, then cut, tested, and packaged.

📖 Worked example — CPU time and speedup, computed

WORKED EXAMPLE — the performance equation in action
CPU time = instructions × CPI × clock cycle time (or ÷ clock rate).

Program: 2 billion instructions, CPI = 2, clock = 4 GHz.
CPU time = (2×10⁹ × 2) / (4×10⁹) = 1 second.
A new compiler cuts instructions to 1.6×10⁹ but CPI rises to 2.2:
time = (1.6×10⁹ × 2.2) / 4×10⁹ = 0.88 s → speedup = 1 / 0.88 ≈ 1.14×.
All three factors matter — improving one while worsening another can still win or lose. Always recompute the whole product.
⚠️ MHz/GHz ALONE NEVER DECIDES
A 3 GHz CPU with CPI 4 is slower than a 2 GHz CPU with CPI 1 on the same instruction count. And Amdahl’s Law caps any speedup by the fraction you DIDN’T improve: speeding up 80% of a program infinitely still leaves the other 20% → max 5×.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Architects optimize what they can measure. Performance has many faces — response time, throughput, energy, cost — and the right metric depends on the workload. Knowing the metrics, the iron law of CPU performance, and how to compare designs honestly is foundational to every architectural decision.

Core concepts

1. Response time vs throughput. Response time (latency): how long one request takes. Critical for interactive workloads. Throughput: requests per unit time. Critical for batch and server workloads. Improving one sometimes hurts the other; design choices target which matters.

2. CPU execution time. Wall-clock time the CPU spends executing a program. Includes user CPU time and system CPU time. Excludes I/O wait. Architecture optimizations target this. Profiling tools (perf, top) report it.

3. Clock cycles, clock period, clock rate. Clock period: time per cycle (e.g., 0.5 ns). Clock rate (frequency): cycles per second (e.g., 2 GHz). Period and rate are reciprocals. Older designs raced for higher clock rates; modern ones balance other factors.

4. The iron law of CPU performance. CPU time = Instructions × CPI × Clock period. To make code faster, reduce instruction count (better algorithms, compiler optimization), reduce CPI (better microarchitecture, pipelining), or shorten clock period (faster transistors). Architects work all three levers.

5. CPI — Cycles Per Instruction. Average cycles each instruction takes. Simple instruction: maybe 1 cycle. Memory access: 100+ cycles on cache miss. Branch misprediction: 10-20 cycles. CPI is averaged over the workload; can be measured per program with profiling.

6. Benchmarks for comparing systems. Specific programs run on candidate systems and compared. SPEC CPU for general-purpose performance. SPEC Power for energy. TPC for databases. LINPACK for floating-point on supercomputers. Each measures different things; never compare without knowing the benchmark.

7. Power and energy. Power: watts (joules per second). Energy: joules. Energy = Power × Time. Performance per watt is the dominant metric in mobile and data centers. Two designs may have the same speed but very different energy consumption.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Comparing systems by clock rate alone — modern CPUs at 3 GHz vary dramatically in actual speed.
  • Optimizing instruction count without measuring CPI — fewer instructions can be slower if they have higher CPI.
  • Reporting only one benchmark — different benchmarks favor different designs.
  • Confusing power and energy — a 100W chip running for 1 second uses the same energy as a 50W chip running for 2 seconds.

Quick recap

Performance has many dimensions: response time, throughput, energy, cost. CPU time = Instructions × CPI × Clock period — the iron law. Clock rate alone doesn't determine speed; CPI varies wildly with cache behavior, branch prediction, and instruction mix. Use standard benchmarks (SPEC, TPC, LINPACK) for honest comparisons. Power vs energy distinction matters for mobile and server workloads.

Glossary

Response time (latency)
Time for a single operation to complete.
Throughput
Operations completed per unit time.
CPI (Cycles Per Instruction)
Average number of clock cycles each instruction takes.
Iron law of performance
CPU time = Instructions × CPI × Clock period.
Benchmark
Standardized program for measuring and comparing computer performance.

Amdahl’s Law: speedup is limited by the serial fraction — Speedup = 1 / ((1 − P) + P/N), where P is the parallelizable fraction and N the processor count. Even infinite processors cannot beat 1/(1 − P). Measured speedup = base_time / new_time — old over new, a ratio bigger than 1 when you actually got faster.

📊 FIGURE — which mean for which job
🎯 EXAM TIP
For combining benchmark scores across a suite, use the geometric mean: it weights ratio improvements equally, so one benchmark with huge absolute numbers cannot dominate the summary. It is the industry standard for benchmark suites (SPEC among them) precisely because the result does not change when you change the reference machine.

Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the steps, in order

📖 Worked example — compile a statement into MIPS-style instructions

WORKED EXAMPLE — f = (g + h) − (i + j)
add $t0, $s1, $s2    # t0 = g + h
add $t1, $s3, $s4    # t1 = i + j
sub $s0, $t0, $t1    # f  = t0 − t1
Each instruction does ONE operation with THREE register operands (two sources, one destination) — the RISC design principle “simplicity favors regularity.” Registers ($s0-$s7 for variables, $t0-$t9 for temporaries) are the fastest storage: only 32 of them, so the compiler juggles.
⚠️ OPERANDS ARE REGISTERS, NOT MEMORY
In a load-store (RISC) architecture, arithmetic never touches memory directly — data must be LOADED into registers first, computed on, then STORED back. That separation is the next section’s whole story.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Every program a CPU runs is, at its lowest level, a sequence of instructions. Each instruction is a tiny task: add two numbers, load a value from memory, jump to a different point in the code. Understanding the structure of instructions — their operations (what to do) and operands (what to do it to) — is the gateway to reading assembly, debugging crashes inside library code, writing efficient compilers, and reasoning about CPU performance. The RISC-V ISA used in C952 has been deliberately designed to make this structure as clean as possible.

The anatomy of an instruction

Every instruction has two parts:

  1. Operation (opcode): WHAT to do — add, subtract, load, store, branch
  2. Operands: WHAT to do it on — register names, memory addresses, immediate constants

Example RISC-V instruction:

add  x5, x6, x7
 ^    ^   ^   ^
 op  dst src1 src2

This says: "Take the value in register x6, add the value in register x7, write the result to register x5." All in one clock cycle.

The three operand classes

1. Registers

RISC-V has 32 general-purpose integer registers, named x0 through x31. Each holds a 32-bit value (RV32) or 64-bit value (RV64). Registers are the FASTEST storage in the CPU — accessed in a single clock cycle.

  • x0 is hardwired to ZERO. Writing to x0 is a no-op; reading it always gives 0.
  • x1 through x31 are free for the compiler to use, subject to calling-convention rules.
  • Registers have nicknames: x1 = ra (return address), x2 = sp (stack pointer), x5–x7 = t0–t2 (temporaries), x10–x17 = a0–a7 (arguments), and so on.

Why only 32? More registers = more bits to encode them = bigger instructions = bigger code. 32 hits the sweet spot for most workloads.

2. Memory addresses

Memory is bigger and slower than registers. Memory operands appear in just two instructions:

lw   x5, 0(x6)    # LOAD WORD: read 32 bits from address (x6+0) into x5
sw   x5, 0(x6)    # STORE WORD: write x5's 32 bits to address (x6+0)

The notation 0(x6) means "the address computed as register x6 plus the constant 0." This is the only way RISC-V accesses memory: base register + immediate offset.

3. Immediate constants

An immediate is a literal number embedded directly in the instruction:

addi  x5, x6, 100   # x5 = x6 + 100  (the 100 is immediate)

Immediates are limited in size by the instruction encoding. In RISC-V, most I-type immediates are 12 bits, giving a range of -2048 to +2047. Bigger constants require two instructions to build.

The RISC philosophy: load/store architecture

RISC-V is a load/store architecture: arithmetic happens ONLY on registers. To add two numbers from memory, you must:

  1. LOAD each value into a register
  2. ADD the registers
  3. STORE the result back to memory (if needed)
# C code:    a = b + c;
# Assume a, b, c are at memory addresses 0(x10), 4(x10), 8(x10):
lw   x5, 4(x10)    # load b
lw   x6, 8(x10)    # load c
add  x7, x5, x6    # add
sw   x7, 0(x10)    # store to a

Why force this? Because keeping arithmetic and memory access in separate instructions makes the CPU simpler to build AND easier to pipeline. Compare to x86, where ADD [rax+4], rbx does both at once but is much harder to implement efficiently.

Operation categories

CategoryExamplesWhat they do
Arithmeticadd, sub, mul, divMath on register values
Logicaland, or, xor, notBitwise ops
Shiftsll, srl, sraShift bits left/right
Comparisonslt, sltuSet register to 1 if less-than, else 0
Memorylw, sw, lb, sb, lh, shLoad / store word, byte, halfword
Branchbeq, bne, blt, bgeConditional jump
Jumpjal, jalrUnconditional jump, often for function calls
Systemecall, ebreakOS call, debugger break

Instruction formats

RISC-V instructions are all 32 bits wide (in the base ISA). The 32 bits are divided into fields that encode the opcode, the operands, and any immediate. There are 6 formats:

  • R-type (register-only): add, sub, and, or, xor, slt, ... — 3 register operands
  • I-type (immediate): addi, andi, lw, jalr, ... — 2 registers + 12-bit immediate
  • S-type (store): sw, sb, sh — 2 registers + 12-bit immediate (split)
  • B-type (branch): beq, bne, blt, ... — 2 registers + 13-bit immediate (split, scaled by 2)
  • U-type (upper-immediate): lui, auipc — 1 register + 20-bit immediate
  • J-type (jump): jal — 1 register + 21-bit immediate (split, scaled by 2)

The reason for separate formats: each instruction class needs different numbers of registers and different immediate sizes. Splitting into formats lets each one use its 32 bits most efficiently while keeping the decoder fast.

Why these constraints matter

The reason RISC-V instructions are uniformly 32 bits wide, with regular fields and only a few formats:

  • Easy decoding: the CPU can decode any instruction in a single cycle without complex parsing
  • Pipelining: uniform width means the next instruction is always at PC+4
  • Compilability: compilers can pick instructions easily without complex addressing modes to worry about
  • Predictability: easy to count cycles and reason about performance

x86 instructions, by contrast, range from 1 to 15 bytes. Decoding them is genuinely complex (Intel CPUs have multi-stage decoders that translate x86 to internal RISC-like micro-ops).

Reading instructions: a concrete example

A C statement:

// Assume i is in x5, sum is in x6, and arr[] is at memory address in x10
sum = sum + arr[i];

In RISC-V:

slli x7, x5, 2     # x7 = i × 4  (each int is 4 bytes; shift left by 2 = multiply by 4)
add  x7, x10, x7   # x7 = base address + offset = &arr[i]
lw   x8, 0(x7)     # x8 = arr[i]
add  x6, x6, x8    # sum = sum + arr[i]

4 instructions for what looked like a single line of C. This expansion happens for EVERY statement — and is what compilers do for you, billions of times.

★ A KEY INTUITION

In a load/store architecture like RISC-V, EVERY memory access requires a separate instruction. This makes assembly verbose, but it makes the hardware simpler and faster. Most modern CPUs (even x86 internally) use load/store designs under the hood, exposing the older complex-instruction interface only for backward compatibility.

Pseudo-instructions

Some convenient operations are built from one or two real instructions. The assembler recognizes them and expands them automatically. Examples:

PseudoReal expansion
mv x5, x6addi x5, x6, 0
li x5, 100addi x5, x0, 100
nopaddi x0, x0, 0
not x5, x6xori x5, x6, -1
retjalr x0, x1, 0

Pseudo-instructions make assembly readable without expanding the ISA. The CPU never sees them — only the real expansions.

✓ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Every instruction has an operation (opcode) and one or more operands
  • Operands come in three classes: registers, memory addresses, immediates
  • RISC-V is load/store: arithmetic uses registers; only LW and SW touch memory
  • RISC-V has 32 integer registers (x0–x31); x0 is hardwired to zero
  • Instructions are uniformly 32 bits, in one of 6 formats (R, I, S, B, U, J)
  • Immediates are limited in size by their format (typically 12 bits for I-type)
  • Pseudo-instructions are convenience names for common patterns; the assembler expands them
  • Reading assembly is a skill — each high-level line typically expands to 2–10 instructions

📖 Worked example — loads, stores & array indexing

WORKED EXAMPLE — g = h + A[8]
lw  $t0, 32($s3)     # t0 = A[8]   (8 words × 4 bytes = offset 32,
                     #              base address of A in $s3)
add $s1, $s2, $t0    # g = h + t0
The addressing mode base+offset: address = $s3 + 32. Words are 4 bytes, so element i lives at base + 4i — forgetting the ×4 is THE classic error. sw (store word) mirrors lw to write back: sw $s1, 48($s3) puts g into A[12].
⚠️ lw DESTINATION FIRST, sw SOURCE FIRST
lw $t0, 32($s3) reads memory INTO the register; sw $t0, 32($s3) writes the register into memory — same syntax shape, opposite direction. Exams love asking which way the data flows.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Memory is where your data lives. The CPU has tiny, ultra-fast registers — maybe 32 of them — but a program has millions or billions of values to track. Those values live in memory, and getting them in and out efficiently is one of the largest performance factors in modern computing. How instructions name memory locations (the addressing modes) determines the cost, complexity, and flexibility of every access. RISC-V's addressing model is deliberately minimal; understanding it lets you read assembly cleanly and grasp why cache locality matters so much.

The memory model

Think of memory as one giant array of bytes, numbered from 0 to (memory size − 1). Each byte has a unique address. Values larger than 1 byte (16-bit halfwords, 32-bit words, 64-bit doublewords) occupy consecutive byte addresses.

Address:  0x1000  0x1001  0x1002  0x1003  0x1004  0x1005  ...
Byte:     [ 0xAB ][ 0xCD ][ 0xEF ][ 0x12 ][ 0x34 ][ 0x56 ]...
                                     ^
                          A 32-bit word at address 0x1000 = 0x12EFCDAB (little-endian)

Byte ordering: little-endian vs big-endian

When a multi-byte value is stored at address A, which byte is at A — the least significant or the most significant?

  • Little-endian: least-significant byte FIRST (at lowest address). x86, ARM (default), RISC-V.
  • Big-endian: most-significant byte first. Network protocols, older mainframes, some embedded.

The value 0x12345678 stored at address 0x1000 in little-endian:

0x1000: 0x78    (least significant byte)
0x1001: 0x56
0x1002: 0x34
0x1003: 0x12    (most significant byte)

Why little-endian? It makes type conversion easier: a 32-bit value's least significant byte is at the same address as the 8-bit value you'd get by ignoring the upper 24 bits. Lets you cast pointers without arithmetic.

Alignment

Most architectures require that multi-byte loads be aligned: a 4-byte word must start at an address divisible by 4; an 8-byte doubleword at an address divisible by 8.

  • Aligned (LW from address 0x1000, 0x1004, 0x1008): single memory transaction.
  • Unaligned (LW from 0x1001): may require two memory transactions OR trigger a hardware exception.

RISC-V technically allows unaligned access but it can be MUCH slower on simple implementations and may be unsupported entirely on embedded chips. Always align your data.

RISC-V's addressing model: just one mode

RISC-V intentionally has ONLY ONE memory addressing mode: base register + sign-extended 12-bit immediate offset.

lw   x5, 16(x6)    # address = x6 + 16
sw   x5, -4(x10)   # address = x10 + (-4) = x10 - 4

That's it. Every memory access has the form imm(reg). No multi-register indexing, no scaled offsets, no auto-increment, no segment registers.

Why so minimal? Simplicity in hardware, ease of pipelining, and clean compiler code generation. Combined operations like arr[i*4] are built from explicit shift and add instructions, which keeps each instruction's job small.

Common addressing patterns in RISC-V

1. Simple variable access

# int x; — x lives at memory address in x10
lw   x5, 0(x10)    # load x into register x5

2. Struct field access

struct Point { int x; int y; int z; };
# p is a pointer in register x10
# &p->y is at offset 4 (since x is at offset 0, takes 4 bytes)
lw   x5, 4(x10)    # load p->y

3. Array indexing

# int arr[10]; — arr base in x10, index i in x6, want arr[i]
slli x7, x6, 2     # x7 = i * 4 (sizeof int)
add  x7, x10, x7   # x7 = &arr[i]
lw   x5, 0(x7)     # x5 = arr[i]

This 3-instruction pattern is so common that x86 has a special "scaled index" addressing mode for it (mov eax, [rbx + rcx*4]). RISC-V keeps the steps explicit, which makes the cost obvious.

4. Stack frame access

# Locals live at fixed offsets from sp (x2). For example,
# the second local int is at offset -8 from sp:
lw   x5, -8(sp)

5. Constant pool access (PC-relative)

For larger constants or jump targets that don't fit in an immediate, the compiler uses auipc (Add Upper Immediate to PC) plus an offset:

auipc x5, %hi(label)    # x5 = (PC + high 20 bits of label offset)
lw    x6, %lo(label)(x5) # x6 = *(label)

Load instructions: more than just LW

InstructionSize loadedSign-extends?
lb — load byte8 bitsYes
lbu — load byte unsigned8 bitsNo (zero-extends)
lh — load halfword16 bitsYes
lhu — load halfword unsigned16 bitsNo
lw — load word32 bitsYes (RV64), N/A (RV32)
lwu — load word unsigned32 bitsNo (RV64 only)
ld — load doubleword64 bitsN/A (RV64 only)

Sign-extension matters: if you load a signed byte 0xFF (= −1) with lb, the register holds 0xFFFFFFFF (= −1). With lbu, it holds 0x000000FF (= 255). Picking the wrong variant is a classic bug.

Store instructions

Stores are simpler (no sign-extension needed):

  • sb — store byte (low 8 bits)
  • sh — store halfword (low 16 bits)
  • sw — store word (low 32 bits)
  • sd — store doubleword (RV64 only)

Address space layout

The OS gives each process a virtual address space organized into regions:

RegionWhat's thereGrows
TextCompiled instructions (read-only)Fixed
DataInitialized globals/staticsFixed
BSSUninitialized globals (zero-filled)Fixed
Heapmalloc'd / new'd objectsUp ↑
StackFunction frames, locals, return addressesDown ↓

Heap grows toward higher addresses; stack grows toward lower. They approach each other from opposite ends, with the OS or hardware preventing collision (a stack overflow is when the stack runs into the heap).

⚠ NULL POINTER ACCESS

Address 0 (the NULL pointer) is deliberately left unmapped in most operating systems. Accessing it triggers a segmentation fault — that's how the OS catches dereferencing null. If you see lw x5, 0(x6) and the program crashes, x6 may be holding null (zero).

Memory speed hierarchy (preview)

Even though all memory looks like one giant byte array to the programmer, accessing it varies wildly in speed:

TierCapacityAccess time
Registers~32 entries< 1 ns
L1 cache~32 KB~1 ns
L2 cache~256 KB~4 ns
L3 cache~16 MB~12 ns
Main memory (DRAM)~16 GB~100 ns
SSD~1 TB~50 μs (50,000 ns)
Hard disk~10 TB~10 ms (10,000,000 ns)

The same LW instruction can take 1 ns (L1 hit) or 100 ns (cache miss) or 10 ms (page fault). Reasoning about WHERE your data lives is huge.

✓ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Memory is a giant byte-addressable array, indexed from 0 to (size − 1)
  • Multi-byte values occupy consecutive bytes; byte order is little-endian on RISC-V/x86/ARM
  • Alignment matters: align to the size of the access (4-byte word at 4-byte boundaries)
  • RISC-V has ONE addressing mode: imm(reg) = base register + 12-bit signed immediate
  • Load instructions: lb/lbu/lh/lhu/lw/lwu/ld differ in size and sign-extension
  • Store instructions: sb/sh/sw/sd; no sign-extension question
  • Address space layout: text, data, BSS (fixed) + heap (grows up) + stack (grows down)
  • NULL (address 0) is unmapped — dereferencing it segfaults
  • Memory speed varies 10,000,000× from registers to disk — locality is everything

📊 FIGURE — the steps, in order

📖 Worked example — a procedure call, stack and all

WORKED EXAMPLE — calling square(5)
li   $a0, 5          # argument goes in $a0
jal  square          # jump-and-link: $ra = return address
...                  # result comes back in $v0

square:
addi $sp, $sp, -4    # grow the stack (it grows DOWN)
sw   $s0, 0($sp)     #   save the register we'll clobber
mul  $v0, $a0, $a0   # v0 = a0 * a0
lw   $s0, 0($sp)     #   restore
addi $sp, $sp, 4     # shrink the stack back
jr   $ra             # return to the caller
The contract: arguments in $a0-$a3, results in $v0-$v1, return address in $ra (set by jal, used by jr). Saved registers ($s0-$s7) must be preserved — that’s what the stack push/pop is for.
⚠️ NESTED CALLS MUST SAVE $ra
If square called another procedure, jal would overwrite $ra and the way home would be lost — so non-leaf procedures push $ra on the stack first. “Why save $ra?” is the section’s most-tested question.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Functions (procedures) are the unit of code reuse. Calling one looks trivial in a high-level language — x = square(7); — but underneath, the CPU has to save its place, hand over arguments, run the callee, retrieve a result, and restore its state. The rules for HOW that happens are called the calling convention. Understanding the call sequence and the stack lets you debug crashes inside library calls, write efficient code, understand security exploits like stack smashing, and read disassembly from any program. C952 covers this in depth because every nontrivial program lives or dies by its function calls.

What needs to happen during a call

When function main calls function square(x):

  1. The caller must REMEMBER where to come back to (the return address).
  2. The caller must HAND OVER the argument (the value of x).
  3. Control must JUMP to the start of square.
  4. Inside square, it computes its result (x*x).
  5. square must HAND BACK the result.
  6. Control must JUMP back to where main left off.

The calling convention specifies exactly HOW each of these happens. Every program on a given platform follows the same convention, so code from different sources can interoperate.

The RISC-V calling convention

Register names (ABI nicknames)

RegisterNicknameRole
x1raReturn address (set by jal)
x2spStack pointer
x3gpGlobal pointer
x4tpThread pointer
x5–x7t0–t2Temporaries (caller-saved)
x8s0/fpSaved register / frame pointer
x9s1Saved register
x10–x11a0–a1Arguments / return values
x12–x17a2–a7Arguments only
x18–x27s2–s11Saved registers
x28–x31t3–t6More temporaries

Caller-saved vs callee-saved

  • Caller-saved (t0–t6, a0–a7): the callee can clobber these freely. If the caller needed them preserved, the CALLER must save them before the call.
  • Callee-saved (s0–s11): the callee MUST save and restore these. The caller can rely on s-registers being preserved across the call.

This split is a tradeoff: caller-save is cheap when the caller doesn't need the values; callee-save is cheap when the callee doesn't use those registers. Compilers pick based on which values live longer.

The call/return sequence — concrete example

A C function:

int square(int x) {
    return x * x;
}

int main() {
    int y = square(7);
    return y;
}

Assembly for square

square:
    mul  a0, a0, a0    # return value goes in a0
    ret                # = jalr x0, ra, 0 (jump to address in ra)

That's the entire function. No stack frame needed because square uses only one register (a0) and doesn't call anyone else.

Assembly for main

main:
    addi  sp, sp, -16   # allocate 16 bytes of stack
    sw    ra, 12(sp)    # save return address
    li    a0, 7         # set argument a0 = 7
    jal   ra, square    # call square; ra ← PC+4 (the return point)
    # On return, a0 holds the result (49)
    lw    ra, 12(sp)    # restore return address
    addi  sp, sp, 16    # deallocate stack
    ret                 # return to whoever called main

The stack frame

A function's stack frame holds its local variables, saved registers, and any arguments that didn't fit in registers (when there are more than 8 args).

High address
    +---------------------+
    | caller's frame      |
    +---------------------+
    | extra arguments     |  (args 9, 10, ...)
    +---------------------+ ← old sp (caller's)
    | saved ra            |
    | saved s0 (fp)       |
    | other saved regs    |
    | local variables     |
    +---------------------+ ← new sp (callee's)
Low address

Stacks grow DOWNWARD. The function decrements sp to allocate space (addi sp, sp, -N) and increments it before returning (addi sp, sp, +N).

The full prologue/epilogue pattern

For any function that calls other functions or uses callee-saved registers:

Prologue (entry)

foo:
    addi sp, sp, -32       # reserve stack space
    sw   ra,  28(sp)       # save return address
    sw   s0,  24(sp)       # save callee-saved regs we'll use
    sw   s1,  20(sp)
    # ... function body ...

Epilogue (exit)

    # ... function body continues ...
    lw   s1,  20(sp)       # restore callee-saved regs
    lw   s0,  24(sp)
    lw   ra,  28(sp)       # restore return address
    addi sp, sp, 32        # release stack
    ret                    # back to caller

Note: the prologue/epilogue are mirror images. Last in, first out — classic stack discipline.

Argument passing

Arguments go in a0 through a7 (8 registers). The first integer argument is in a0, second in a1, and so on. Beyond 8 args, the rest go on the stack (above the caller's sp).

Return values:

  • A single integer return value goes in a0.
  • Two integer return values (rare) go in a0, a1.
  • Larger return values: caller passes a pointer to space; callee writes through it.

jal and jalr — the call/return primitives

  • jal rd, label: jump to label, save (PC+4) into register rd. By convention, rd = ra (x1). PC+4 is the address of the instruction RIGHT AFTER the call — exactly where we want to return.
  • jalr rd, rs1, imm: jump to (rs1 + imm), save (PC+4) into rd. Used for indirect calls (function pointers, return-from-function via ra).

Common idioms:

PseudoRealMeaning
call foojal ra, fooStandard function call
retjalr x0, ra, 0Return; result discarded
j labeljal x0, labelUnconditional jump, no save

Recursive calls and the stack

Recursion works because each recursive call gets its OWN stack frame. When factorial(5) calls factorial(4), both have separate frames with their own locals and saved ra. The stack grows deeper; recursion unwinds by popping frames in reverse order.

factorial:
    addi sp, sp, -16
    sw   ra, 12(sp)        # save ra
    sw   s0,  8(sp)        # save s0 (we'll use it)
    li   t0, 1
    bge  t0, a0, base      # if n <= 1, return 1
    mv   s0, a0            # save n
    addi a0, a0, -1        # arg = n-1
    jal  ra, factorial     # recursive call
    mul  a0, a0, s0        # result = n * factorial(n-1)
    j    done
base:
    li   a0, 1
done:
    lw   ra, 12(sp)
    lw   s0,  8(sp)
    addi sp, sp, 16
    ret

Each recursive level pushes 16 bytes (ra + s0 + padding). For n=5, the stack grows 80 bytes deep before unwinding.

⚠ STACK OVERFLOW

Infinite or deep recursion exhausts stack space and the program crashes. The default stack size on Linux is 8 MB — typically enough for a few thousand to tens of thousands of frames depending on frame size. Tail-call optimization (where the compiler reuses the current frame for a tail-recursive call) is one way to avoid this, but the C standard doesn't require it.

Stack smashing — a security concern

If a function copies user input into a local buffer without bounds checking, the input can overflow into the saved ra, letting an attacker overwrite it with the address of attacker-supplied code. This is a stack-buffer overflow ("stack smashing").

Modern defenses:

  • Stack canaries: a random value placed between locals and saved ra; checked before ret. If corrupted, abort.
  • Non-executable stack (NX bit): stack memory marked non-executable so attacker shellcode won't run.
  • ASLR: randomize the stack address each run so attackers can't predict where to jump.

These defenses aren't perfect — return-oriented programming (ROP) bypasses NX by chaining existing code snippets — but they raise the cost of attacks dramatically.

✓ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Function calls require: saving the return address, passing args, jumping, returning a result, restoring state
  • RISC-V uses jal ra, label to call and ret (= jalr x0, ra, 0) to return
  • Arguments go in a0–a7; return values in a0 (and a1 for pairs)
  • Caller-saved registers (t0–t6, a0–a7): the callee may clobber; caller must save if needed
  • Callee-saved registers (s0–s11): the callee must save/restore; caller can rely on them
  • Stack frames hold saved registers, locals, and overflow arguments — built in the function prologue, torn down in the epilogue
  • The stack grows DOWNWARD; sp decreases on entry, increases on exit
  • Recursion works by giving each call its own frame
  • Stack smashing — overflowing a buffer into saved ra — was historically the #1 security exploit

The MIPS stack grows DOWNWARD — toward lower addresses. Pushing subtracts from the stack pointer ($sp) then stores; popping loads then adds back. “Grows down, push subtracts” is the two-second recall.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — one instruction, down to the bits

WORKED EXAMPLE — encode add $t0, $s1, $s2 (R-format)
| op(6) | rs(5) | rt(5) | rd(5) | shamt(5) | funct(6) |
|  000000 | 10001 | 10010 | 01000 |  00000  | 100000 |
    op=0     $s1=17   $s2=18   $t0=8    0       add=32
Every MIPS instruction is exactly 32 bits. R-format packs three registers; I-format (lw/sw/beq/addi) swaps the last three fields for a 16-bit immediate; J-format gives 26 bits of jump target. The op field tells the hardware which layout to read — machine code is just these fields glued together.
⚠️ STORED PROGRAM = INSTRUCTIONS ARE NUMBERS
That 32-bit pattern sits in memory like any data — the computer can’t tell “code” from “numbers” except by what it fetches. This is the stored-program concept, asked on every architecture exam.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Machine instructions are 32-bit binary patterns. Their encoding determines what fields exist and where. Reading binary instructions back into assembly (disassembly) and computing branch targets requires understanding the formats. It's the lowest level of program representation before raw electrical signals.

Core concepts

1. MIPS R-type format (32 bits). opcode (6) | rs (5) | rt (5) | rd (5) | shamt (5) | funct (6). All register-to-register operations. The opcode is 0 for R-types; the funct field distinguishes add, sub, and, etc. Five bits per register field gives 32 registers.

2. MIPS I-type format. opcode (6) | rs (5) | rt (5) | immediate (16). For instructions with a 16-bit immediate or address: addi, lw, sw, beq. The immediate is signed; range -32768 to 32767.

3. MIPS J-type format. opcode (6) | address (26). For unconditional jumps: j, jal. The 26-bit address is shifted left 2 bits (instructions are word-aligned), then combined with the high 4 bits of PC. Effective range: 256 MB.

4. Calculating branch target addresses. beq, bne use PC-relative addressing. Target = (PC + 4) + (immediate × 4). The immediate is a signed offset in instructions, not bytes — multiply by 4 (word size) to get the byte offset. Range: PC ± 128 KB.

5. Calculating jump target addresses. j, jal use pseudo-direct addressing. Target = (PC[31:28]) | (address × 4). The 26-bit address × 4 gives 28 low bits; the 4 high bits come from the current PC. Limits jumps to within a 256 MB region.

6. Opcode and function fields. The opcode (6 bits) selects the instruction type. For R-types, opcode is 0 and the funct (6 bits) selects the specific operation. This split allows many instructions while keeping the format consistent. Decoding hardware uses opcode first, then funct if needed.

7. From assembly to machine code. The assembler translates each assembly instruction to its 32-bit binary. Symbolic labels are resolved to addresses. Pseudo-instructions (`move $t0, $t1` becomes `add $t0, $zero, $t1`) are expanded. The resulting binary is exactly what the CPU executes.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Forgetting branch offsets are in instructions, not bytes — off by 4x in target calculations.
  • Confusing the 16-bit immediate's signed range with unsigned — addi can't reach addresses above 32K from zero.
  • Treating jump target as absolute — it's pseudo-direct (high 4 bits from PC).
  • Confusing opcode and funct for R-types — opcode is 0; funct distinguishes the specific R-type operation.

Quick recap

MIPS instructions are 32 bits in three formats: R (register-to-register), I (immediate or memory), J (jump). Opcode picks the type; funct (R-types only) picks the specific operation. Branches use PC-relative addressing scaled by 4. Jumps use pseudo-direct addressing combining the address field with high PC bits. Assemblers translate human-readable assembly to these exact binary patterns.

Glossary

R-type instruction
MIPS format for register-to-register operations: opcode | rs | rt | rd | shamt | funct.
I-type instruction
MIPS format for immediate/memory operations: opcode | rs | rt | immediate.
J-type instruction
MIPS format for jumps: opcode | address (26-bit).
PC-relative addressing
Branch target = PC + offset; used by beq, bne.
Opcode
Field in an instruction selecting the operation; first 6 bits in MIPS.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Integer arithmetic is the simplest CPU operation and the place every architectural decision starts. Understanding two's complement, how the ALU adds and subtracts, and what overflow means is foundational. Most modern code is built on this; exploits often start with overflow bugs.

Core concepts

1. Two's complement representation. Binary representation where the most significant bit signals sign. Positive numbers: standard binary. Negative numbers: invert all bits and add 1. -1 is all ones (0xFFFFFFFF for 32-bit). Range: -2^31 to 2^31 - 1. The dominant signed integer encoding for 50+ years.

2. Why two's complement. Addition and subtraction work uniformly on signed and unsigned. 5 + (-3) = 0...0101 + 1...1101 = 0...0010 = 2. Just bits; no special signed adder needed. Compare to sign-magnitude (negative numbers have a sign bit), which needed separate logic. Two's complement won.

3. Overflow in signed addition. Adding two positives can produce a negative; adding two negatives can produce a positive. 0x7FFFFFFF + 1 = 0x80000000 (most negative). The CPU's overflow flag detects this. Software may ignore it (C doesn't trap) or check it explicitly.

4. Overflow vs carry-out. In unsigned: carry-out from the top bit signals overflow (the result doesn't fit). In signed (two's complement): overflow is when sign bit changes unexpectedly — the XOR of carry-in and carry-out at the top bit. Different conditions; the CPU tracks both with separate flags.

5. Subtraction is addition of negative. a - b = a + (-b) = a + (NOT b) + 1. The CPU implements subtraction by inverting b and setting carry-in to 1. Same adder hardware does both. ARM and MIPS implementations differ in details but follow the same idea.

6. The ALU — Arithmetic Logic Unit. Hardware block performing arithmetic and logic. Inputs: two operands plus a control signal selecting the operation. Output: result plus condition flags (zero, negative, overflow, carry). One ALU per pipeline stage; the centerpiece of integer execution.

7. When overflow matters in real code. Signed integer overflow in C/C++ is undefined behavior — compilers may assume it doesn't happen and optimize accordingly. Integer overflow vulnerabilities are a real attack class — buffer size calculations that overflow, leading to undersized allocations and exploits beyond. Treat with care.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Assuming signed overflow wraps in C — it's undefined behavior; the compiler may eliminate checks based on this assumption.
  • Confusing carry-out with signed overflow — different conditions in different contexts.
  • Ignoring the most-negative number's special case — its negation overflows.
  • Expecting `int` to be a particular width — it's typically 32 bits but not guaranteed.

Quick recap

Two's complement encodes signed integers so the same hardware adds signed and unsigned. Negation: invert all bits, add 1. Overflow in signed: sign changes unexpectedly. Subtraction is addition of the negation. The ALU performs arithmetic, logic, and comparisons with control inputs. Real-world integer overflow bugs are a significant security concern, especially in C/C++.

Glossary

Two's complement
Standard binary signed integer encoding; negation = invert bits + 1.
Signed overflow
When a signed addition or subtraction produces a result outside the representable range.
Carry-out
Bit emitted when an addition exceeds unsigned range.
ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit)
Hardware block performing arithmetic, logic, and comparisons.
Undefined behavior
C/C++ language rule: signed overflow has no defined result; compilers may exploit this.

Sign-extension widens a signed number by replicating the sign bit into the new upper bits (1011 → 11111011 for 8 bits). A ripple-carry adder propagates the carry bit-by-bit — simple but slow, since each stage waits for the previous carry. A carry-lookahead adder computes carries in parallel from the inputs, trading extra gates for speed. To negate in two’s complement: invert every bit and add 1 (5 = 0101 → 1010 + 1 = 1011 = −5).

Hex view of sign-extension: 16-bit 0xFFFD (−3) widened to 32 bits becomes 0xFFFFFFFD — the F digits are the replicated sign bits. Zero-padding to 0x0000FFFD would turn −3 into 65533: a corrupted value, not a widened one.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — 8-bit two’s complement: 100 + 50, then 100 − 50
PART 1 — 100 + 50 in 8 bits
    0110 0100   =  100
  + 0011 0010   =   50
  -----------
    1001 0110   =  150 unsigned, but -106 signed
  c3 (carry INTO the top bit) = 1 , c4 (carry OUT) = 0
  unsigned overflow = c4        = 0  -> no unsigned overflow (150 fits in 0..255)
  signed   overflow = c3 XOR c4 = 1  -> SIGNED OVERFLOW (150 > 127)

PART 2 — 100 - 50, done as 100 + (-50)
  -50 = NOT(0011 0010) + 1 = 1100 1101 + 1 = 1100 1110  = 0xCE
    0110 0100   =  100
  + 1100 1110   =  -50
  -----------
  1 0011 0010   -> discard the 9th bit
    0011 0010   =   50   correct
  c4 = 1, c3 = 1 , so c3 XOR c4 = 0 -> no signed overflow

Output: 100 + 50 = -106 (signed overflow); 100 - 50 = 50 (correct)

Two lessons live in this one page of bits. First, the SAME adder did both operations — subtraction is just addition of the inverted operand with carry-in 1. Second, the carry out lied twice: in Part 1 it was 0 while the signed answer was ruined, and in Part 2 it was 1 while the signed answer was perfect. The trap is treating the carry flag as an error light. For unsigned values the carry out IS the overflow signal; for two’s complement you must XOR the carry into the top bit with the carry out of it — or, equivalently, check whether two operands of the same sign produced a result of the opposite sign.

Figure — the carry out of the MSB flags UNSIGNED overflow; XOR-ing it with the carry INTO the MSB flags SIGNED overflow. Adding numbers of opposite sign can never overflow.

📊 FIGURE — the steps, in order

📖 Worked example — binary multiplication by shifts

WORKED EXAMPLE — 6 × 5 the hardware way
  0110  (6)
× 0101  (5)
------
  0110        ← 5's bit0 = 1: add 6, shifted 0
 0000         ← bit1 = 0: skip
011000        ← bit2 = 1: add 6 shifted left 2 (=24)
------
011110  = 30 ✓
Binary long multiplication = for each 1-bit of the multiplier, add a shifted copy of the multiplicand. Shift-left by k = ×2ᵏ — which is why compilers turn ×8 into <<3. Division mirrors it with shift-and-subtract, producing quotient + remainder; and dividing by zero traps (hardware exception).
⚠️ PRODUCT NEEDS DOUBLE WIDTH
Multiplying two 32-bit numbers can need 64 bits — MIPS parks the result in the HI/LO register pair. Overflow questions on multiplication are really “did you remember the width doubles?”
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Addition and subtraction are fast — typically one cycle. Multiplication is harder; division is significantly harder still. Understanding the algorithms and circuits the CPU uses for these operations explains why x / y takes 20–40 cycles when x + y takes 1, why compilers replace divisions with shifts whenever possible, and why integer overflow can silently corrupt arithmetic. This section covers the algorithms used inside the CPU and the practical implications for performance and correctness.

Multiplication: shift-and-add

Long multiplication taught in school works in any base. For binary:

      1011    (= 11)
    × 1101    (= 13)
    ------
      1011    ← 1011 × 1
     0000     ← 1011 × 0, shifted left 1
    1011      ← 1011 × 1, shifted left 2
   1011       ← 1011 × 1, shifted left 3
   --------
   10001111   (= 143 ✓ 11 × 13)

Each bit of the multiplier contributes either 0 or the multiplicand (shifted appropriately). For N-bit operands, you get N partial products and a final addition of all of them.

Hardware implementation

A naive shift-and-add multiplier:

  1. Init: product = 0; counter = N
  2. If multiplier's LSB is 1, add multiplicand to product (upper half of accumulator)
  3. Shift product right by 1 (and shift multiplier right by 1)
  4. Decrement counter
  5. If counter > 0, go to step 2

This takes N cycles for N-bit operands. For 32-bit values, that's 32 cycles — slow.

Faster: array multipliers

Modern CPUs use an array multiplier (or its variant, a Wallace tree). Instead of one shift-add per cycle, the multiplier generates ALL N partial products in parallel, then sums them with a tree of adders. This produces a 64-bit result from two 32-bit inputs in 3–5 cycles instead of 32.

The cost: a 32-bit array multiplier has ~32² ≈ 1000 full adders. It's a significant chunk of silicon. That's why embedded CPUs often have slower (or no) hardware multipliers, and why floating-point units are even bigger.

RISC-V multiplication instructions

InstructionComputes
mul rd, rs1, rs2rd ← lower 32 bits of (rs1 × rs2)
mulh rd, rs1, rs2rd ← upper 32 bits, signed × signed
mulhu rd, rs1, rs2rd ← upper 32 bits, unsigned × unsigned
mulhsu rd, rs1, rs2rd ← upper 32 bits, signed × unsigned

To get the full 64-bit product of two 32-bit values, you do mul for the low half and mulh for the high half. The reason for separate instructions: keeping each result fits in 32 bits matches the register width.

Overflow in multiplication

If you multiply two 32-bit values and write the lower 32 bits to a register, any bits that would have gone above 32 are silently DROPPED. mul never traps; you get truncated wraparound.

0x10000 × 0x10000 = 0x100000000   (33 bits)
mul result = 0x00000000           (low 32 bits — overflow!)
mulh result = 0x00000001          (high 32 bits)

Languages handle this differently:

  • C / C++: signed overflow is undefined behavior; unsigned wraps. Either way, the compiler may not check.
  • Java: silently wraps (defined behavior).
  • Python: integers are arbitrary precision; overflow doesn't happen.
  • Rust: traps in debug builds, wraps in release builds (unless you use checked_mul).

Strength reduction: replacing × with shifts

Multiplying by a power of 2 is the same as shifting left:

x * 8     ≡ x << 3
x * 16    ≡ x << 4
x * 1024  ≡ x << 10

Multiplying by some non-power-of-2 constants can be done with a few shifts and adds:

x * 5  = x * 4 + x       = (x << 2) + x        // 2 ops vs 1 mul
x * 10 = x * 8 + x * 2   = (x << 3) + (x << 1) // 3 ops vs 1 mul

Compilers do this automatically when they see multiplication by a known constant. It's called strength reduction.

Division: longer and harder

Long division in binary works just like decimal: subtract repeatedly, recording quotient bits. The standard restoring division algorithm:

  1. Init: remainder = dividend (extended), quotient = 0, counter = N
  2. Shift remainder left by 1
  3. Try to subtract divisor from upper half of remainder
  4. If result ≥ 0: remainder = result, quotient = (quotient << 1) | 1
  5. If result < 0: leave remainder, quotient = quotient << 1
  6. Decrement counter; if > 0, go to step 2

This takes N cycles for N-bit operands. Unlike multiplication, division resists parallelization — each iteration depends on the previous one's comparison. Most CPUs have 20–40 cycle latency for integer divide.

RISC-V division instructions

InstructionComputes
div rd, rs1, rs2rd ← rs1 / rs2 (signed)
divu rd, rs1, rs2rd ← rs1 / rs2 (unsigned)
rem rd, rs1, rs2rd ← rs1 % rs2 (signed)
remu rd, rs1, rs2rd ← rs1 % rs2 (unsigned)

Special cases

RISC-V division does NOT trap on edge cases — instead, it returns defined values:

  • Divide by zero: quotient = all 1s (= -1 for signed, max value for unsigned); remainder = dividend
  • Overflow (most-negative ÷ -1): quotient = most-negative; remainder = 0

This is unlike x86 (which traps with #DE on divide-by-zero). Software must check zero divisor explicitly if it wants an error.

Strength reduction: replacing ÷ with shifts

Dividing by a power of 2 is the same as shifting right:

x / 8     ≡ x >> 3   (for unsigned)

For SIGNED integers, you need an arithmetic right shift (sra) AND a rounding correction (because shifting rounds toward negative infinity, while integer division rounds toward zero in C/Java).

Division by a constant: clever optimization

Even non-power-of-2 division by a constant can be replaced with a multiplication and a shift. For example:

// Replace x / 10 with:
x * 0xCCCCCCCD >> 35    // approximate reciprocal

This trick lets compilers turn slow division into fast multiplication, getting 5×–10× speedups. Use Compiler Explorer to see your compiler do this automatically.

Modulo (remainder)

x % y is mathematically related to x / y by: x % y = x - (x / y) * y. Most CPUs compute both q and r simultaneously since they fall out of the same algorithm.

One important use: x % 2 == 0 tests evenness. The compiler often replaces this with x & 1 == 0, which is a single-cycle AND instead of a 20-cycle DIV.

Floating-point: a different beast

Floating-point multiplication and division use entirely different circuits than integer ops. Multiplication is roughly equivalent in cost to integer multiplication; floating-point division is significantly slower and goes through a different unit (often with iterative Newton-Raphson approximation). We cover this in the next section.

Performance impact

OperationTypical latency (cycles)
add, sub, and, or, xor1
sll, srl, sra (shift)1
mul (integer)3–5
div, rem (integer)20–40
fmul (float)3–5
fdiv (float, double precision)10–25
fsqrt (float)10–25

Division being 20–40× slower than addition is why algorithm authors often go to great lengths to avoid division (e.g., precomputing reciprocals, using bit tricks, choosing data structures that don't need it).

✓ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Integer multiplication uses an array multiplier — 3–5 cycle latency on modern CPUs
  • Integer division is much slower (20–40 cycles) because each iteration depends on the previous
  • RISC-V provides mul, mulh, mulhsu, mulhu to get all of a 64-bit product from two 32-bit operands
  • RISC-V provides div, divu, rem, remu; divide-by-zero returns defined values (no trap)
  • Overflow on mul truncates silently; software must check if needed
  • Strength reduction: compilers replace multiplication or division by constants with shifts and adds
  • Division by a constant can be replaced by multiplication by a reciprocal — a 5–10× win
  • Modulo with power-of-2 (x % 2^k) reduces to a bitwise AND (x & (2^k − 1))
  • Floating-point divide and sqrt are even slower; design algorithms to avoid them when possible

TermDefinition
Normalized formthe mantissa is always between 1 and 2, so the leading 1 is IMPLICIT (not stored).
Biased exponentthe exponent is stored as actual_exp + 127 (single) or +1023 (double), so comparison can use unsigned integer compare.

Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the steps, in order

📖 Worked example — decode an IEEE 754 float

WORKED EXAMPLE — what is 0 | 10000001 | 0100…0 ?
Single precision = 1 sign + 8 exponent (bias 127) + 23 fraction bits.
• sign 0 → positive.
• exponent 10000001₂ = 129 → actual exponent = 129 − 127 = 2.
• fraction .01₂ → significand = 1.01₂ = 1.25 (the leading 1 is implicit!).
Value = 1.25 × 2² = 5.0.
Encoding runs the same recipe backwards: normalize to 1.xxx × 2ᵉ, add 127 to e, drop the leading 1.
⚠️ THE HIDDEN 1 AND THE BIAS
Two traps: the significand’s leading 1 is NOT stored (add it back when decoding), and the exponent field holds e + 127 (subtract the bias). Special patterns: exponent all-0s → zero/denormals; all-1s → ±infinity/NaN.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Floating-point numbers are how computers represent non-integer values: 3.14, 1.5e-10, 6.022e23. They're a tradeoff — finite hardware can't represent infinitely many real numbers, so floating-point is an approximation. Every programmer encounters their surprises: 0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3 exactly, subtracting almost-equal numbers loses precision, comparing for equality breaks. Understanding the IEEE 754 standard explains why these happen and how to work around them. Critical for scientific computing, graphics, machine learning, finance — anywhere math is approximate.

The IEEE 754 standard

IEEE 754 (1985, revised 2008 and 2019) defines floating-point formats and operations. Almost every CPU, GPU, and language now follows it, so floating-point math is portable across hardware. Two main formats matter for C952:

FormatTotal bitsSignExponentMantissa~Range
Single (float)321823±10⁻³⁸ to ±10³⁸
Double6411152±10⁻³⁰⁸ to ±10³⁰⁸

Double-precision is the default in most modern languages (e.g., Python's float, JavaScript's Number, Java's double).

The encoding: sign, exponent, mantissa

A floating-point number is stored as three fields:

Single precision (32 bits):
[s | exponent (8 bits) | mantissa (23 bits)]
 ^                        ^
 1 sign bit               23 fractional bits

Value = (−1)ˢ × 1.mantissa × 2^(exponent − 127)

Three key tricks:

  1. Normalized form: the mantissa is always between 1 and 2, so the leading 1 is IMPLICIT (not stored). You get one free bit of precision.
  2. Biased exponent: the exponent is stored as actual_exp + 127 (single) or +1023 (double), so comparison can use unsigned integer compare.
  3. Sign bit: just one bit. 0 = positive, 1 = negative. Same magnitude either way (so 0.0 and -0.0 both exist but compare equal).

Example: encoding 6.5

Step 1: Convert 6.5 to binary. 6.5 = 110.1₂

Step 2: Normalize. 110.1 = 1.101 × 2². Mantissa = 101, exponent = 2.

Step 3: Bias the exponent. 2 + 127 = 129 = 10000001₂.

Step 4: Combine. Sign = 0 (positive); exponent = 10000001; mantissa = 10100000000000000000000 (pad to 23 bits).

0 10000001 10100000000000000000000
= 0x40D00000

Verify: (−1)⁰ × 1.101₂ × 2² = 1.625 × 4 = 6.5 ✓

Special values

IEEE 754 reserves certain exponent encodings for special values:

Exponent fieldMantissaRepresents
All zerosZeroZero (+0 or −0)
All zerosNon-zeroSubnormal (tiny number, gradual underflow)
All onesZeroInfinity (+∞ or −∞)
All onesNon-zeroNaN (Not a Number)
OtherwiseAnyNormal number

Why 0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3

Binary floating-point cannot exactly represent decimal fractions that aren't powers-of-2 combinations. 0.1 in binary is 0.000110011001100… repeating forever — like 1/3 in decimal. Truncated to 52 bits of mantissa, it becomes a very close BUT NOT EXACT value. The same applies to 0.2.

When you compute 0.1 + 0.2, each operand was already rounded, and the sum is rounded again. The result is approximately 0.30000000000000004, off by about 5×10⁻¹⁷.

>>> 0.1 + 0.2
0.30000000000000004
>>> 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3
False

This is not a bug in any language. It's a consequence of binary representation. To compare floats, use a tolerance: abs(a - b) < 1e-9.

Precision and significant digits

  • Single precision: 23 mantissa bits + 1 implicit = ~7 decimal significant digits.
  • Double precision: 52 mantissa bits + 1 implicit = ~16 decimal significant digits.

Beyond these limits, floats simply can't distinguish two adjacent values. For double: 10¹⁶ and 10¹⁶ + 1 may store the same.

Precision pitfalls

1. Catastrophic cancellation

Subtracting two nearly-equal numbers throws away most of the significant digits:

a = 1.0000001
b = 1.0000000
a − b = 0.0000001   // only 1 significant digit left

Numerical algorithms are designed to avoid this. The classic example: the quadratic formula (-b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a loses precision when 4ac is tiny. Use the algebraically-equivalent 2c / (-b ∓ √(b² − 4ac)) for the smaller root.

2. Comparing floats for equality

NEVER use == with floats. Use a tolerance (epsilon):

// Bad:
if (x == 0.1) { ... }

// Good:
if (Math.abs(x - 0.1) < 1e-9) { ... }

3. Accumulating error in loops

double sum = 0.0;
for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) sum += 0.1;
// Expected: 100000.0; actual: ~99999.9999986

Each iteration's rounding error accumulates. For large sums, use Kahan summation or higher-precision intermediates.

4. NaN propagation

Any arithmetic involving NaN produces NaN. NaN + 1 = NaN. NaN > 0 = false. NaN < 0 = false. NaN == NaN = false. This last one is the easiest way to detect NaN: x != x is true iff x is NaN.

Floating-point operations on RISC-V

The base RISC-V ISA doesn't include floating-point — it's added by the F (single-precision) and D (double-precision) extensions. With these, you get 32 floating-point registers (f0–f31) and instructions like:

  • fadd.s rd, rs1, rs2 — float add
  • fmul.d rd, rs1, rs2 — double multiply
  • fdiv.d rd, rs1, rs2 — double divide
  • fsqrt.s rd, rs1 — single square root
  • flw rd, off(rs1) — load single from memory
  • fsd rd, off(rs1) — store double

Most have a fused multiply-add form: fmadd.d rd, rs1, rs2, rs3 computes rs1×rs2+rs3 with only one rounding, giving slightly better accuracy than a separate multiply and add.

Performance

OperationLatencyThroughput
fadd, fmul3–5 cycles1/cycle
fdiv (double)10–25 cycles1 per 5–15 cycles
fsqrt (double)10–25 cyclesSame

Multiplications and adds are fast and pipelined. Divisions and sqrt are slow and don't pipeline well — algorithm design typically minimizes them.

When to AVOID floating-point

  • Money / currency: use fixed-point or decimal types. Floats can't represent 0.10 exactly, and rounding errors are unacceptable.
  • Counting: always use integers. Float counters lose precision past 2²⁴ (single) or 2⁵³ (double).
  • Exact comparisons: integer-only logic preferred when possible.
  • Hash keys, indices: never use floats as map keys.
✓ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • IEEE 754 is the universal standard for floating-point representation
  • A float is (−1)ˢ × 1.mantissa × 2^(biased_exp − bias)
  • Single = 32 bits, ~7 significant decimal digits; Double = 64 bits, ~16 digits
  • Special values: ±0, ±∞, NaN, subnormals — all encoded via reserved exponent fields
  • 0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3 because decimal fractions like 0.1 are infinite repeating in binary
  • Never compare floats with ==; use a tolerance
  • NaN is contagious: it propagates through arithmetic; detect with x != x
  • Catastrophic cancellation: subtracting near-equal numbers destroys precision
  • Float division and sqrt are 5–10× slower than add/mul
  • Never use floats for money, counting, or exact comparisons
