📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — floating-point addition, step by step

WORKED EXAMPLE — 1.5 × 2² + 1.0 × 2⁰
1. Align exponents: shift the smaller — 1.0 × 2⁰ becomes 0.01 × 2².
2. Add significands: 1.50 + 0.25 = 1.75.
3. Result: 1.75 × 2² = 7.0 ✓ (6 + 1). Renormalize and round if needed.

Align → add → normalize → round is the full pipeline. The rounding step is why floating-point math is APPROXIMATE: 0.1 has no exact binary form, so 0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3 exactly.
⚠️ FP ADDITION ISN’T ASSOCIATIVE
(big + tiny) + tiny can differ from big + (tiny + tiny) — small values vanish when aligned against a huge exponent. That’s why parallel FP sums can give slightly different answers depending on order — a real exam question.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Floating-point arithmetic is more complex than integer because the operands have different scales. Adding requires aligning exponents; multiplying requires combining them. The hardware (FPU) handles this, but rounding choices and edge cases are visible to software in the form of precision loss and unexpected results.

Core concepts

1. Floating-point addition algorithm. Align: shift the smaller operand's mantissa right to match the larger's exponent. Add: add mantissas. Normalize: shift to put the leading 1 in the right position; adjust exponent. Round: drop excess bits. Each step takes time; FP add is roughly the same latency as FP multiply (~3-5 cycles on modern CPUs).

2. Floating-point multiplication algorithm. Multiply mantissas (treating them as fractions). Add exponents (subtract bias to avoid double-counting). Normalize result. Round. The XOR of sign bits gives the result's sign. Conceptually simpler than addition; just as fast in modern hardware.

3. Rounding modes. IEEE 754 defines several. Round to nearest (even on tie): the default. Round toward zero: truncate. Round toward +infinity, toward -infinity: directional. Affects last-bit precision; matters in numerical code where many operations accumulate. Switchable via FPU control register.

4. Guard, round, and sticky bits. During calculations, the hardware keeps extra bits below the visible mantissa: guard (next bit), round (one after), sticky (OR of all further bits). These determine rounding direction. Without them, every operation would round prematurely and cumulative error would explode.

5. Precision loss in subtraction. Subtracting two nearly-equal floats can lose most of the precision (catastrophic cancellation). Example: 1.0001 - 1.0000 = 0.0001 — a 4-digit input produces a 1-digit result. Numerical methods are designed to avoid this; naive code falls into it constantly.

6. Order of operations matters. Floating-point addition is NOT associative. (a + b) + c ≠ a + (b + c) in general. Sums of many small numbers can lose precision. Kahan summation algorithm preserves precision by tracking the running error. Numerical libraries use it; naive sums don't.

7. FPU — Floating-Point Unit. Dedicated hardware for floating-point arithmetic. Pipelined so throughput is one operation per cycle on common ops. SIMD extensions (AVX, NEON) execute multiple FP operations in parallel. Modern CPUs have many FPUs.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Summing many small numbers naively — accumulated error makes result far less accurate than expected.
  • Subtracting nearly-equal floats — catastrophic cancellation destroys precision.
  • Comparing FP with == — already covered, but worth repeating.
  • Reordering FP operations for optimization — changes results; compilers respect this with -fno-fast-math by default.

Quick recap

FP addition: align exponents, add mantissas, normalize, round. FP multiplication: multiply mantissas, add exponents, normalize, round. Rounding modes affect last-bit precision; default is round-to-nearest-even. Guard/round/sticky bits prevent premature rounding. Subtraction can lose precision (catastrophic cancellation); sums are non-associative; Kahan summation preserves accuracy in long chains. The FPU executes all of this; SIMD extends to multiple values per cycle.

Glossary

Alignment (FP)
Shifting the smaller operand's mantissa to match exponents before addition.
Normalization
Shifting result to put the implicit leading 1 in the right position; adjust exponent.
Guard, round, sticky bits
Extra bits below the visible mantissa that determine rounding direction.
Catastrophic cancellation
Severe precision loss when subtracting nearly-equal floating-point values.
FPU
Floating-Point Unit — dedicated hardware for FP arithmetic.

Floating-point edges: overflow — the result exceeds the max representable and becomes ±infinity; underflow — the result is smaller than the smallest normal number and degrades toward zero. Never compare floats with ==: accumulated rounding makes exact equality fragile — test abs(a − b) < epsilon instead.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — one instruction’s trip through the datapath

WORKED EXAMPLE — follow add $t0, $s1, $s2 through the hardware
1. PC feeds the instruction memory → the 32-bit instruction comes out.
2. The rs/rt fields select $s1, $s2 in the register file → two values read.
3. The ALU adds them.
4. The result writes back to $t0 in the register file; PC + 4 points at the next instruction.

A lw takes the longer road: register + offset through the ALU → data memory read → write-back. A beq computes PC + offset and a comparison chooses which address the mux feeds the PC. Every instruction is just a different route through the same five pieces (PC, instruction memory, registers, ALU, data memory) — with muxes doing the routing.
⚠️ MUXES ARE THE ANSWER TO “HOW DOES IT CHOOSE?”
Whenever two sources could feed one input (ALU’s second operand: register or immediate? PC’s next value: +4 or branch target?), a multiplexer selects — steered by control signals. Datapath questions are almost always “which mux, which signal?”
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Building a CPU starts with the datapath — the wiring of components that move data and produce results. The single-cycle datapath is the simplest design: one clock cycle per instruction. Slow but conceptually clean. Knowing each component (PC, register file, ALU, memory) and its role is the foundation for understanding pipelining.

Core concepts

1. The Program Counter (PC). 32-bit register holding the address of the next instruction. Updated each cycle: usually PC + 4 (to next instruction) but jumped on branches and jumps. Foundation of sequential execution. Every CPU has one (or many in superscalar designs).

2. Instruction memory. Stores the program. Indexed by PC. Output: the 32-bit instruction at that address. In real CPUs, instruction memory is the L1 instruction cache backed by main memory; in textbook designs, it's a simple memory block.

3. The register file. 32 registers, each 32 bits. Two read ports (so an instruction can read two source registers in one cycle) and one write port (write a result back). Register file is the fastest storage; the heart of register-based ISAs.

4. The ALU — Arithmetic Logic Unit. Performs add, subtract, AND, OR, set-less-than, shift, and so on. Two 32-bit inputs plus a 4-bit control signal selecting the operation. Output: 32-bit result plus a zero flag (used for branches). Center of every datapath.

5. Data memory. Stores program data — variables, arrays, the heap, stack. Loads read from it; stores write to it. Like instruction memory, a simple block in textbook design; an L1 data cache backed by main memory in real hardware.

6. Multiplexers (muxes). Select among multiple inputs based on a control signal. Datapath uses muxes to: pick between PC+4 and branch target; pick register vs immediate as ALU input; pick ALU result vs memory data as the value to write back. Muxes are how the datapath flexibly handles different instruction types.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Confusing instruction memory and data memory — both store bytes but serve different roles in the architecture.
  • Forgetting that the register file has two read ports and one write port — a single port would serialize instruction execution.
  • Treating the ALU as opaque — knowing its operations and control signals is essential for understanding instruction execution.
  • Mixing up sign extension and zero extension — wrong choice gives wrong arithmetic results.

Quick recap

Single-cycle datapath: PC drives instruction memory. Instruction read out splits into fields. Register file reads source registers. ALU computes. Result either goes to data memory or back to the register file. Muxes pick paths; sign extension expands immediates. Each instruction completes in one clock cycle; cycle must be long enough for the slowest instruction.

Network of components and connections that move and process data in a CPU.
Program Counter (PC)
Register holding the address of the next instruction.
Register file
Bank of registers with multiple read and write ports.
Multiplexer (mux)
Selector circuit choosing among multiple inputs based on a control signal.
Sign extension
Expanding a smaller signed value to a larger size by replicating the sign bit.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Datapath components are wired together, but they need control signals to do the right thing for each instruction. The control unit generates these signals from the opcode. Understanding the instruction cycle — fetch, decode, execute, memory, write-back — and the control signals that drive each stage is how a CPU actually executes code.

Core concepts

1. The five classic stages. Fetch (IF): read instruction from instruction memory at PC. Decode (ID): break instruction into fields, read register file. Execute (EX): ALU performs the operation. Memory (MEM): load or store, if applicable. Write-back (WB): write result to register file. Single-cycle does all in one cycle; pipelined does each in a different cycle.

2. Control signals. Each component has control inputs: ALU operation (4 bits), register write enable, memory read/write enables, mux selectors. The control unit generates them based on the instruction's opcode (and funct for R-types).

3. The control unit as combinational logic. Inputs: 6-bit opcode (and 6-bit funct for R-types). Outputs: ~10 control signals. Implemented as a truth table or PLA (Programmable Logic Array). For each instruction type, a row in the table specifies which signals are 1 and which are 0.

4. R-type instruction's path. Fetch instruction. Decode: read rs and rt from register file. Execute: ALU computes (e.g., add). Memory: skip. Write-back: write result to rd. Control signals: RegWrite=1, ALUSrc=0 (use register, not immediate), MemRead=0, MemWrite=0, MemtoReg=0, RegDst=1 (use rd, not rt).

5. Load instruction's path. Fetch. Decode: read rs (base) and rt (target). Execute: ALU adds rs + sign-extended immediate. Memory: read data memory at the computed address. Write-back: write to rt. Control: RegWrite=1, ALUSrc=1 (use immediate), MemRead=1, MemtoReg=1, RegDst=0 (use rt).

6. Branch instruction's path. Fetch. Decode: read rs and rt. Execute: ALU subtracts to compare. Memory: skip. Write-back: skip. PC update: if zero flag set (operands equal), PC = PC + 4 + (offset × 4); else PC = PC + 4. Control: Branch=1, RegWrite=0.

Multi-cycle: each instruction takes multiple cycles, but each cycle is shorter. Pipelining (next chapter) overlaps stages of different instructions for the best of both.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS

  • Mixing control signal conventions — each textbook may use slightly different names.
  • Trying to handle every instruction without a control table — quickly becomes intractable; the table is the systematic approach.
  • Confusing single-cycle (one clock per instruction) with multi-cycle (multiple short clocks per instruction) — different design philosophies.

Quick recap

Each instruction follows a five-stage path: fetch, decode, execute, memory, write-back. The control unit translates opcodes (and functs) into the control signals each stage needs. R-type, load, store, and branch instructions follow different paths through the same datapath, distinguished by control signals. Single-cycle is conceptually clean but wastes time; pipelining fixes that.

Glossary

Instruction cycle
Sequence of stages (IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB) executing one instruction.
Control unit
Combinational logic generating control signals from the instruction's opcode.
Control signal
Single-bit (or multi-bit) input to a datapath component selecting its behavior.
Fetch / Decode / Execute
First three stages: get instruction, parse it, perform ALU operation.
Single-cycle CPU
Design where each instruction completes in one (long) clock cycle.

“Why not single-cycle?” → the clock is set by the LONGEST path, wasting time on short instructions. Pipelining (next chapter) fixes it by cutting the work into stages and overlapping instructions.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Single-cycle CPUs are conceptually simple but slow. Understanding why — the clock period is dictated by the slowest instruction — motivates pipelining. The performance analysis of single-cycle is the baseline against which all faster designs measure themselves.

Core concepts

1. Clock period limits. The clock period must be long enough for the slowest instruction to complete. In MIPS single-cycle, that's the load: fetch + decode + ALU + memory access + write-back. ~600-800 ps total. Even an add (no memory access) waits the full cycle. Wasteful.

2. The critical path. The longest signal-propagation path through the datapath. From PC, through instruction memory, through register file read, through ALU, through data memory, through register file write. Architects work to minimize the critical path; clock period equals critical path delay.

3. Why single-cycle is wasteful. Different instruction types have very different critical paths. Add: ~400 ps (no memory). Load: ~700 ps. The clock must be 700 ps for everything; the add wastes 300 ps every cycle. Across millions of adds, that's significant.

4. Multi-cycle alternative. Each instruction takes multiple shorter cycles. Add: 4 cycles; load: 5 cycles. Clock period now determined by the slowest single stage (~200 ps), not the slowest entire instruction. Average CPI > 1 but clock period much shorter; usually a wash, slightly slower.

5. Pipelining as the better answer. Overlap stages of different instructions. While one instruction is in WB, another is in MEM, another in EX, another in ID, another in IF. CPI approaches 1 (best case); clock period is the slowest single stage. Best of both worlds — when the pipeline doesn't stall.

6. The CPI-clock period tradeoff. The iron law (CPU time = Inst × CPI × Period) lets you trade. Single-cycle: CPI = 1, Period long. Multi-cycle: CPI > 1, Period short. Pipelined: CPI ≈ 1, Period short (best). Each design chooses a point on the tradeoff.

7. Real CPUs are deeply pipelined. Modern CPUs have 10-20 stage pipelines and out-of-order execution. The concepts compound: more stages, more hazards, more complexity, but more parallelism. Single-cycle is a teaching device, not a competitive design.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Comparing CPU designs only by clock rate — a 3 GHz multi-cycle CPU with CPI=4 is slower than a 2 GHz pipelined one with CPI=1.5.
  • Forgetting that the critical path determines clock period — speeding up most instructions doesn't help if the critical instruction stays slow.
  • Treating single-cycle CPUs as practical — they're educational; no real CPU is built this way.
  • Conflating multi-cycle and pipelined — different designs with different trade-offs.

Quick recap

Single-cycle CPUs have one cycle per instruction. Clock period equals the critical path length, set by the slowest instruction. Wasteful for fast instructions. Multi-cycle breaks the cycle into shorter ones (CPI > 1, shorter period). Pipelining overlaps stages of different instructions (CPI ≈ 1, shorter period). The iron law: CPU time = Instructions × CPI × Period. Real CPUs are pipelined.

Glossary

Clock period
Time per clock cycle; reciprocal of clock rate.
Critical path
Longest signal-propagation path; determines minimum clock period.
Multi-cycle CPU
Design with multiple cycles per instruction but shorter per-cycle delay.
Pipelining
Overlapping stages of different instructions to approach 1 instruction per cycle throughput.
Throughput vs latency
Instructions per second vs time per single instruction; pipelining maximizes throughput.

WORKED EXAMPLE — 5 stages, 4 instructions, count the cycles

cycle:    1   2   3   4   5   6   7   8
instr 1:  IF  ID  EX  MEM WB

Four instructions finish by cycle 8 instead of 4 × 5 = 20. Once the pipe is full, one instruction completes every cycle — throughput ≈ 5× better, even though each individual instruction still takes 5 stages (latency unchanged!). Just like washer/dryer/folding overlapping loads of laundry.
⚠️ THROUGHPUT UP, LATENCY NOT
Pipelining does NOT make one instruction faster — it makes the STREAM faster. Ideal speedup = number of stages; hazards (next sections) are what keep it below ideal. That distinction is the #1 exam question.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Pipelining is the technique that turned slow single-cycle CPUs into the high-throughput processors we have today. Five stages overlapping in time means five instructions in flight simultaneously — ideally one finishing per cycle. It's the single biggest performance idea in mainstream CPU design.

Core concepts

1. The five stages overlapping. IF (Instruction Fetch), ID (Instruction Decode and register read), EX (Execute / ALU), MEM (Memory access), WB (Write-Back to register file). At any cycle, five different instructions occupy the five stages. Output: roughly one instruction per cycle.

2. Pipeline registers between stages. Between each pair of stages: a register holding the partial state. IF/ID register, ID/EX register, EX/MEM register, MEM/WB register. Each cycle, values shift forward. Pipeline registers are what make stages independent and allow concurrent execution.

3. Ideal speedup. If the pipeline is full and never stalls, throughput is one instruction per cycle. Compared to single-cycle (1 instruction per long cycle), the speedup is roughly the number of stages — 5x for five stages. Compared to multi-cycle, speedup is even more dramatic.

4. Pipeline latency vs throughput. Latency: time for one instruction to complete (5 cycles). Throughput: instructions completing per cycle (ideally 1). Pipelining doesn't speed up individual instructions; it speeds up the rate of completion. Latency stays the same; throughput multiplies.

5. Why CPI = 1 is the ideal. In a 5-stage pipeline, after the first 4 cycles (filling the pipeline), one instruction completes per cycle. CPI of 1 is the throughput-equivalent of one instruction per cycle. Deviations come from hazards (next sections); each hazard forces a stall, increasing effective CPI.

6. Pipeline fill and drain. First 4 cycles: pipeline filling, no instructions complete yet. Last 4 cycles: pipeline draining. For long programs, fill and drain are negligible; for short ones, they're noticeable. Branch mispredictions cause similar fill/drain costs throughout execution.

7. The reality of modern pipelines. Modern CPUs have 10-20 stages with out-of-order execution and superscalar issue (multiple instructions per cycle). The concepts compound — same hazards, more handling. Five stages is a teaching baseline; production designs are far deeper and wider.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Confusing latency and throughput — a 5-stage pipeline doesn't complete one instruction in 1 cycle; it completes one per cycle on average.
  • Forgetting that pipelining requires pipeline registers — these add latency to each stage and area to the chip.
  • Assuming CPI = 1 always — hazards push it above 1; superscalar designs push it below 1.
  • Treating the 5-stage pipeline as the only design — modern CPUs are far more complex.

Quick recap

Pipelining overlaps stages of different instructions. Five stages: IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB. Pipeline registers between stages hold partial state. Ideal CPI is 1; throughput is dramatically higher than single-cycle. Latency for individual instructions stays the same. Hazards push CPI above 1; deeper pipelines and superscalar issue push throughput further. The dominant CPU performance idea since the 1980s.

Glossary

Pipelining
Overlapping the execution stages of multiple instructions to increase throughput.
Pipeline register
Storage between two pipeline stages holding the partial instruction state.
IF/ID/EX/MEM/WB
The five classic MIPS pipeline stages.
Throughput vs latency
Instructions completed per cycle vs time for a single instruction.
Pipeline fill/drain
Initial cycles before the pipeline is full and final cycles after the last instruction enters.

📖 Worked example — a data hazard, stalled vs forwarded

WORKED EXAMPLE — add then immediately use the result
add $s0, $t0, $t1    # $s0 ready after EX (cycle 3)
sub $t2, $s0, $t3    # needs $s0 in ITS EX (cycle 4)!
Without help, sub would read the OLD $s0 in ID — wrong answer or 2-cycle stall. Forwarding wires the ALU’s output straight into the next instruction’s ALU input: the sub gets the fresh value in time, ZERO stalls.

The one case forwarding can’t fix: lw followed immediately by a use — the data arrives from MEM a stage too late, forcing ONE bubble (the load-use hazard). Compilers try to slide an unrelated instruction into that slot.
⚠️ LOAD-USE = ONE UNAVOIDABLE STALL
“Which hazard remains even with full forwarding?” → lw immediately followed by an instruction using the loaded register: 1 bubble, no exceptions. Everything ALU-to-ALU forwards cleanly.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Data hazards happen when one instruction needs the result of an earlier instruction that hasn't yet written back. Without handling, the second instruction reads stale data. Forwarding (bypassing) routes the result directly from where it's computed to where it's needed, avoiding most stalls.

Core concepts

1. RAW (Read-After-Write) hazard. Most common data hazard. Instruction 1 writes a register; instruction 2 (close behind) reads the same register. Without intervention, instruction 2 reads the old value — wrong. Three instructions later, the write completes and the read would have been correct, but it's already too late.

2. The structural picture. add $t0, $t1, $t2 (writes $t0 in WB at cycle 5). sub $t3, $t0, $t4 (reads $t0 in ID at cycle 3). Without forwarding, the sub reads the old $t0. Two cycles too early. Either stall the pipeline (waste cycles) or forward (route the in-flight value).

3. Forwarding (bypassing). The result is available at the EX/MEM register after ALU, and at MEM/WB after memory. Forwarding hardware detects when a later instruction's input matches an earlier instruction's output and routes the value directly from EX/MEM or MEM/WB back to the EX stage's input. No stall needed.

4. The forwarding unit. Compares register sources of the EX-stage instruction against destinations of the EX/MEM and MEM/WB instructions. If matches, the mux selects the forwarded value instead of the register file output. Logic is local; runs every cycle.

5. Load-use hazard — the unsolvable case with forwarding alone. lw $t0, 0($t1) (data available after MEM, end of cycle 4). add $t3, $t0, $t4 (needs $t0 in EX, cycle 3). Even forwarding can't help — the value doesn't exist yet at cycle 3. Solution: stall one cycle. Compiler may also rearrange instructions to fill the slot.

6. The compiler's role. Smart compilers schedule instructions to avoid hazards: insert independent work between dependent instructions. Reduces stall frequency. Modern compilers do this aggressively for instruction scheduling. Combined with hardware forwarding, real CPI is close to 1 in well-scheduled code.

7. WAR and WAW hazards. Write-After-Read and Write-After-Write. In simple in-order pipelines, these don't happen because writes go in order at WB. Out-of-order execution introduces them, and renaming registers at issue time is the standard fix. For 5-stage MIPS, RAW is the only data hazard to worry about.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Forgetting load-use hazards always need a stall — forwarding alone isn't enough.
  • Designing forwarding logic that doesn't catch every case — silent wrong answers.
  • Confusing forwarding with re-executing — forwarding routes existing values; no extra computation.
  • Treating compiler scheduling as optional — without it, even well-forwarded pipelines stall often.

Quick recap

RAW hazards: a later instruction reads a register a recently-issued instruction hasn't written yet. Forwarding routes in-flight values from EX/MEM or MEM/WB back to the EX input, avoiding stalls in most cases. Load-use is the exception: data isn't ready until after MEM, so one stall is needed. Compilers schedule to minimize stalls. WAR/WAW only matter in out-of-order designs; in-order MIPS doesn't see them.

Glossary

Data hazard
Pipeline conflict where an instruction needs data not yet produced.
RAW (Read-After-Write)
Most common data hazard: read of a register before its write completes.
Forwarding (bypassing)
Hardware routing in-flight ALU or memory results to dependent instructions in EX.
Load-use hazard
Hazard where a load's result is needed in the next instruction; requires a 1-cycle stall.
Pipeline stall
Cycle inserted to wait for required data; CPI temporarily above 1.

📖 Worked example — control hazards & branch prediction

WORKED EXAMPLE — what a wrong guess costs
A beq’s outcome isn’t known until it evaluates — but the pipeline already fetched the next instructions. Predict “not taken” and keep fetching:
• Prediction right → zero cost, pipe stays full.
• Prediction wrong → flush the wrongly-fetched instructions (turn them into bubbles) and refetch from the branch target — a penalty of several cycles.

If a branch is taken 90% of the time, a static “predict taken” guess is right 90% of the time; a 2-bit dynamic predictor tracks recent history per branch and adapts — it must be wrong TWICE before flipping its prediction, so an occasional odd iteration (like a loop’s exit) costs only one miss.
⚠️ WHY 2 BITS BEATS 1
A 1-bit predictor mispredicts a loop branch TWICE per loop (once at exit, once re-entering). The 2-bit counter’s “strongly/weakly” states absorb the single anomaly — the standard exam comparison.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Branches are the second major hazard source. The CPU doesn't know whether to take a branch until late — but it needs to fetch the next instruction immediately. Without prediction, every branch costs cycles. Branch prediction has become one of the most important and elaborate parts of modern CPU design.

Core concepts

1. The control hazard. beq $t0, $t1, label. The CPU resolves the branch in EX (cycle 3). But it needs to fetch the next instruction in cycle 2. If the wrong instruction is fetched, it has to be flushed when the branch resolves. 2-3 cycles wasted per branch. With ~20% of instructions being branches, this is significant.

2. Predict-not-taken (default). Simplest prediction: assume the branch is not taken; fetch the next sequential instruction. If correct, no stall. If wrong (branch taken), flush the wrong fetch and start fetching from the target. Cheap; works ~50% on random branches.

3. Branch delay slot — old solution. MIPS originally specified that the instruction immediately after a branch always executes (delay slot). Compiler fills it with a useful instruction. Hardware-simple; software-complex. Modern MIPS deprecates delay slots; modern ISAs (RISC-V, ARM v8+) don't have them.

4. 1-bit dynamic predictor. Remember the last outcome of each branch. Next time, predict the same. Simple table indexed by branch address. Mispredicts twice on every loop boundary (last iteration; first iteration of the next entry to the loop). Around 80% accuracy — better than nothing.

5. 2-bit saturating counter. Each branch has a 2-bit counter. Strongly-not-taken (00), weakly-not-taken (01), weakly-taken (10), strongly-taken (11). Take if 10 or 11. Update on each branch outcome. Takes two consecutive mispredictions to flip prediction. Around 90-95% accuracy on typical code.

6. Branch target buffer. Even if you correctly predict TAKEN, you need the target address. BTB caches the target of recently-taken branches indexed by branch PC. Combined with the predictor, lets you start fetching from the target in the same cycle as the branch.

7. Modern predictors are elaborate. Two-level adaptive predictors, gshare, perceptron predictors, TAGE — research-grade designs reach 95-99% accuracy on real workloads. Misprediction cost is high in deep pipelines (10-20 cycles), so the investment in predictors pays back. State-of-the-art CPUs allocate substantial die area to branch prediction.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Treating branch prediction as static — modern CPUs use dynamic predictors that learn at runtime.
  • Writing code with hard-to-predict branches in hot loops — predictability matters for performance.
  • Forgetting that misprediction cost scales with pipeline depth — modern CPUs pay 10-20 cycles per miss.
  • Optimizing branch prediction without measuring — predictor behavior is hard to reason about; profile.

Quick recap

Branches cause control hazards: pipeline must fetch the next instruction before the branch is resolved. Predict-not-taken is the simplest scheme. Delay slots are an older ISA-level workaround. Dynamic predictors (1-bit, 2-bit, gshare, TAGE) reach 90-99% accuracy. Branch target buffers cache target addresses. Misprediction cost grows with pipeline depth; modern CPUs invest heavily in prediction.

Glossary

Control hazard
Pipeline conflict from branches: next instruction unknown until branch resolves.
Predict-not-taken
Simplest branch prediction: assume the branch is not taken; flush on mispredict.
Branch delay slot
Architectural feature where the instruction after a branch always executes.
2-bit saturating counter
Per-branch state machine with hysteresis between predictions.
Branch Target Buffer (BTB)
Cache of branch target addresses indexed by branch PC.

📖 Worked example — structural hazards & precise exceptions

WORKED EXAMPLE — one memory, two customers
Suppose instructions and data shared ONE memory port. In cycle 4 above, instr 1 is in MEM (reading data) while instr 4 wants IF (fetching) — same resource, same cycle: a structural hazard, forcing a stall.
The fix is hardware: separate instruction/data caches (or more ports) — which is exactly why real CPUs have split L1 I-cache and D-cache.

Exceptions in a pipeline: if instr 2 overflows in EX while instrs 3-4 are already in flight, the CPU must flush the younger ones, finish the older ones, and record the faulting PC — a precise exception — so the OS sees a clean boundary and can resume exactly where things stopped.
⚠️ NAME THE HAZARD FAMILY
Three kinds, three causes: structural = resource conflict; data = value not ready; control = branch outcome unknown. Every hazard question starts by classifying which one you’re looking at.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Beyond data and control hazards, two more pipeline complications: structural hazards (resource conflicts) and exceptions (interrupts and faults). Both force the pipeline to handle situations the simple model didn't anticipate. Knowing how the pipeline copes is foundational to understanding modern processor architecture.

Core concepts

1. Structural hazards — resource conflicts. Two stages in the same cycle want the same hardware. Classic example: instruction memory and data memory share one memory port. IF and MEM stages both try to access in the same cycle. Solution: separate instruction and data memories (Harvard architecture) — what real CPUs do (separate L1 I-cache and D-cache).

2. Single register file write port — and read ports. Register file has two read ports (so ID stage can read two registers at once) and one write port (WB stage writes one register per cycle). If an instruction in WB and an instruction in ID both touch the same register, the write happens in the first half of the cycle and the read in the second half. Standard convention; avoids needing more ports.

3. Exceptions — the unplanned events. Anything that interrupts normal flow: divide by zero, undefined instruction, memory protection violation, hardware interrupt (timer, I/O). Mid-instruction. The CPU must save state, jump to a handler, return when handler is done. Hard in a pipeline.

4. Precise exceptions. When an exception occurs at instruction N, all instructions before N have completed; none after N have. Operating systems and debuggers depend on this. Implementing it in a pipeline requires care: when an exception is detected (typically late, in EX or MEM), all in-flight younger instructions must be flushed.

5. The exception PC (EPC). Special register holding the address of the instruction that caused the exception. After the handler runs, the OS uses EPC to resume — either re-execute the instruction (handle a fault and retry) or skip past it. Architectural state.

6. Pipeline flush on exception. Detected exception at cycle T. Flush all instructions younger than the offender from the pipeline (they were speculatively executed under the assumption no exception would occur). Set PC to the exception handler. Save EPC and other state. Resume in handler context.

7. Exceptions vs interrupts. Exception: synchronous, caused by the current instruction (overflow, page fault, illegal instruction). Interrupt: asynchronous, external (timer, I/O completion). Both follow the same pipeline path — flush, save, jump to handler. Different cause; same mechanism.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Forgetting structural hazards exist — even with separate I/D memories, ports on register files and memory can clash in deeper pipelines.
  • Designing pipelines without precise exceptions — software (OS, debuggers) depends on it.
  • Confusing exceptions and interrupts — same handling, different sources.
  • Treating exception handling as rare — page faults, syscalls, interrupts happen constantly in real systems.

Quick recap

Structural hazards: hardware resource conflicts. Solved by duplication (separate I/D caches) or careful timing. Exceptions: synchronous events from the current instruction. Interrupts: asynchronous external events. Precise exceptions require flushing younger instructions and resuming from EPC. The pipeline must handle these without breaking the abstraction the OS depends on. Real CPUs invest substantial complexity in supporting precise exceptions in deep, out-of-order pipelines.

Glossary

Structural hazard
Pipeline conflict where two stages need the same hardware resource.
Harvard architecture
Separate instruction and data memories; eliminates the I/D structural hazard.
Exception
Synchronous event from the current instruction (fault, trap).
Interrupt
Asynchronous external event (timer, I/O completion).
Precise exception
Property that all instructions before the exception have completed and none after have started.
📊 FIGURE — user mode and kernel mode
🎯 EXAM TIP
Privilege levels are user mode versus kernel mode: kernel mode can do everything, user mode is restricted, and the split is enforced in hardware rather than by the OS asking nicely. Any transition into the kernel goes through a controlled entry point — a system call, interrupt or exception — which is what keeps a user process from doing as it likes.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — locality is why caches work

WORKED EXAMPLE — spot both localities in 3 lines
sum = 0;
for (i = 0; i < n; i++)
    sum += a[i];
• Temporal locality — sum and i are touched EVERY iteration: recently-used things get used again → keep them close (registers/L1).
• Spatial locality — a[0], a[1], a[2]… are neighbors: when a[0] misses, the cache pulls in the whole BLOCK, so a[1]-a[15] hit for free.

The hierarchy (registers → L1 → L2 → L3 → RAM → disk) works because programs behave this way: each level is smaller/faster and holds the recently/nearby-used slice of the one below.
⚠️ BLOCKS EXIST BECAUSE OF SPATIAL LOCALITY
Caches move multi-word BLOCKS, not single bytes, betting neighbors get used. Stride-through-memory access patterns (column-major walks of a row-major array) break the bet — the classic “why is this loop slow?” answer.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Main memory is far slower than the CPU — hundreds of cycles per access. If every memory operation took that long, performance would crater. The memory hierarchy — caches, registers, main memory, disk — exploits locality to make access fast on average. Understanding locality and the hierarchy is foundational to writing fast code.

Core concepts

1. The memory wall. CPU clock rates outpaced memory speed for decades. A modern CPU at 3 GHz issues an instruction every 0.3 ns; main memory access takes 50-100 ns. Without caches, the CPU would idle most of the time. Caches bridge the gap.

2. Temporal locality. Recently-accessed data is likely to be accessed again soon. Loop counters, recently-used objects, frequently-called functions. Cache the recently-accessed; reuse beats re-fetching.

3. Spatial locality. Data near recently-accessed data is likely to be accessed soon. Arrays, structs, instructions in sequence. Cache lines (typically 64 bytes) bring adjacent data on every miss; subsequent nearby accesses hit.

4. The hierarchy levels. Registers: tens, ~1 cycle. L1 cache: tens of KB, ~3-5 cycles. L2: hundreds of KB to few MB, ~10-20 cycles. L3: few to tens of MB, ~30-60 cycles. Main memory: GBs, ~100+ cycles. Storage: TBs, ~10K-100K cycles. Each level smaller, faster, more expensive per byte.

5. Average Memory Access Time (AMAT). AMAT = HitTime + MissRate × MissPenalty. If L1 hits in 4 cycles 95% of the time and miss penalty is 100 cycles: 4 + 0.05 × 100 = 9 cycles. Reducing miss rate or miss penalty has huge effect.

6. Why caches work. Real workloads have locality. Loops touch the same data over and over (temporal). Arrays are processed sequentially (spatial). Without locality, caches couldn't help. Programs that violate locality (random access over large data) suffer.

7. Writing cache-friendly code. Iterate arrays in the order they're stored (row-major in C, column-major in Fortran). Avoid pointer-chasing through linked lists if you can use arrays. Pack frequently-accessed fields into the same cache line. These patterns make a 10x performance difference on memory-bound code.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Optimizing without considering locality — algorithmic improvements lose to cache-unfriendly access patterns.
  • Ignoring AMAT in performance analysis — focusing on cycles per instruction without memory cost misses dominant factor.
  • Treating memory as uniform — different access patterns hit different levels with very different speeds.
  • Iterating arrays in the wrong order — column-major access in C is many times slower than row-major.

Quick recap

Memory hierarchy: registers, L1, L2, L3, main memory, storage. Each level is bigger, slower, cheaper. Caches exploit temporal locality (reuse) and spatial locality (neighbors). AMAT = HitTime + MissRate × MissPenalty captures average cost. Real workloads have locality, which is what makes caches work. Cache-friendly code outperforms cache-unfriendly code dramatically.

Glossary

Memory hierarchy
Layered storage from fast/small (registers, cache) to slow/large (memory, disk).
Temporal locality
Property that recently-accessed data tends to be accessed again.
Spatial locality
Property that data near recent accesses tends to be accessed soon.
AMAT (Average Memory Access Time)
HitTime + MissRate × MissPenalty; the effective access time.
Cache line
Unit of cache transfer; typically 64 bytes; brings spatial neighbors on each miss.

WORKED EXAMPLE — 8-block cache, where does address 0x34 go?
Cache: 8 blocks × 16 bytes. Address 0x34 = 0011 0100₂.
• Offset = low log₂16 = 4 bits → 0100 (byte 4 within the block).
• Index = next log₂8 = 3 bits → 011 (block 3 of the cache).
• Tag = everything left → identifies WHICH memory block sits there.
Lookup: go to index 3, compare the stored tag (+ valid bit) with the address’s tag → match = hit, else miss (fetch the block, replace what’s there).
Direct-mapped = every address has exactly ONE possible slot: index = (block address) mod (number of blocks).

Addresses 0x34 and 0xB4 can share index 3 with different tags — alternate between them and every access misses (conflict misses), even with the rest of the cache empty. That weakness motivates set-associativity (next section).
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Direct-mapped caches are the simplest cache organization. Each memory address maps to exactly one cache slot. Understanding the index/tag/offset breakdown of an address is the foundation for understanding more complex cache designs (set-associative, fully associative).

Core concepts

1. The cache as a small fast memory. A cache holds N blocks (cache lines), each typically 64 bytes. When CPU requests an address, the cache checks if it has the block. Hit: serve from cache. Miss: fetch from memory, install in the cache. The choice of which cache slot to use is the cache organization.

2. Direct-mapped: one slot per index. Each memory block maps to exactly one cache slot. Slot index = (block address) mod (number of slots). If you have 256 slots, block 1000 goes in slot 1000 mod 256 = 232. Block 1256 also goes in slot 232 — they collide. The block currently there gets evicted.

3. Address breakdown: tag, index, offset. 32-bit address splits into three fields. Offset (low bits): byte within the cache line (e.g., 6 bits for 64-byte lines). Index: which slot to use (e.g., 8 bits for 256 slots). Tag: identifies which memory block is in that slot (the rest of the bits — 18 in this example). Cache lookup: take index, fetch slot, compare tags. Match = hit.

4. Why direct-mapped is simple and fast. One slot to check per access. Compare one tag. Output the block if match. Hardware-simple, low latency. The downside: if two frequently-used blocks happen to map to the same slot, they constantly evict each other (conflict misses) — even with empty slots elsewhere in the cache.

5. Calculating cache parameters. Cache size = slots × block size. 256 slots × 64 bytes = 16 KB. Address bits: 6 offset + 8 index + 18 tag = 32 total. Each slot also stores a valid bit (is this slot occupied?) and the tag. Cache hardware area: data + tags + valid bits + comparison logic.

6. Write policies for direct-mapped. Write-through: every write goes to both cache and memory. Simple; slow on writes. Write-back: writes go to cache only; memory updated when the line is evicted. Faster but adds dirty-bit tracking. Real caches use write-back; sometimes a write buffer absorbs the latency.

7. Conflict misses dominate weakness. Direct-mapped's main weakness: two hot blocks mapping to the same slot. Even with 99% empty cache, they ping-pong each other. Set-associative caches (next section) address this by allowing multiple slots per index.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS

  • Forgetting the valid bit — uninitialized slot data masquerades as valid blocks; causes wrong behavior on cold start.
  • Calculating address bits without including offset — block size matters in the tag/index split.
  • Writing performance-sensitive code that accesses two arrays that happen to map to the same direct-mapped cache slots — conflict misses dominate.

Quick recap

Direct-mapped caches map each memory block to exactly one slot. Address breaks into tag, index, offset. Lookup compares the address's tag to the slot's tag. Simple and fast; vulnerable to conflict misses when hot blocks collide. Cache size = slots × block size. Write-through (slow) or write-back (faster, common). Set-associative caches mitigate conflict misses by allowing multiple slots per index.

Glossary

Direct-mapped cache
Each memory block maps to exactly one cache slot.
Cache line / block
Unit of cache transfer; typically 64 bytes.
Tag / Index / Offset
Three fields of an address: tag identifies the block, index picks a slot, offset selects a byte.
Valid bit
Single bit per slot indicating whether the slot's content is meaningful.
Write-through vs write-back
Two write policies: write-through updates memory immediately; write-back defers until eviction.

📖 Worked example — associativity & LRU replacement

WORKED EXAMPLE — same conflict, 2-way sets
In a 2-way set-associative cache, index picks a SET holding 2 blocks — the thrashing pair from last section now COEXIST (one in each way): the ping-pong misses vanish.

Replacement within a set uses LRU: access blocks A, B, A, then C arrives needing a slot → evict B (least recently used; A was refreshed). Fully-associative = one big set, any block anywhere (needs a comparator per block — expensive); direct-mapped = 1-way. Associativity trades hit-rate against hardware cost and hit-time.
⚠️ MORE WAYS ≠ FREE
Doubling associativity cuts conflict misses but adds comparators and can slow the hit path. “Why not fully associative everywhere?” → cost and hit time. Typical real answer: 4-8 way L1.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Direct-mapped caches suffer when two hot blocks collide on the same slot. Set-associative caches give each index multiple slots, drastically reducing conflict misses. The tradeoff: more comparators, slightly more latency. Modern caches are 4-way, 8-way, 16-way set-associative.

Core concepts

1. The set-associative idea. Each cache index has N slots (a 'set'). When a new block comes in, any of the N slots can hold it. To find a block, compare the tag to all N slots in the set. N-way set-associative: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 are typical.

2. Address breakdown changes. Same offset (within block). The number of sets shrinks (cache size / block size / associativity), so fewer index bits. The tag grows correspondingly. For 256-slot cache with 4-way associativity: 64 sets, 6 index bits (vs 8 for direct-mapped), 20 tag bits.

3. Hit logic: compare all ways in parallel. On a lookup, the index picks one set; the cache compares the tag to all N tags in that set in parallel. If any matches AND that slot is valid, hit. Otherwise, miss. The N parallel comparators add area and a tiny bit of latency.

4. Replacement policy: which slot to evict. On a miss into a full set, one of the N slots must be evicted. LRU (Least Recently Used): evict the one not touched for the longest. Best in theory; expensive to implement perfectly for large N. Random: simpler, surprisingly close in practice. NRU (Not Recently Used): cheap LRU approximation.

5. Fully associative — the limit. Any block can go in any slot. No conflict misses ever. Implemented for very small caches (TLBs are typically fully associative). For data caches, the parallel comparison cost (one comparator per slot) makes it impractical at large size.

6. Choosing associativity. Direct-mapped: simplest, fast, conflict-prone. 2-way: cuts conflicts a lot. 4-way: cuts more, common for L1. 8-way to 16-way: typical for L2 / L3. Diminishing returns: going from 4-way to 8-way helps less than 1-way to 2-way. Modern CPUs balance miss reduction against latency and area.

7. Comparing the same cache size. 16 KB direct-mapped: 256 slots, indexed by 8 bits. 16 KB 4-way: 64 sets × 4 slots, indexed by 6 bits. Same total capacity, different conflict behavior. 4-way typically has 30-50% fewer misses on real workloads.

  • Believing more associativity is always better — diminishing returns, and area/latency costs grow.
  • Confusing direct-mapped with fully associative — opposite ends of the spectrum.
  • Implementing 'true LRU' for large associativity — area cost is significant; pseudo-LRU is fine.
  • Designing benchmarks insensitive to cache organization — most code doesn't care; some specific access patterns care a lot.

Quick recap

Set-associative caches give each index N slots. Tag, set-index, offset address breakdown. Hit checks all N tags in parallel. Replacement policy (LRU, random, NRU) picks which slot to evict on miss. Fully associative is the extreme — any slot. 4-way and 8-way are common in real designs. Reduces conflict misses sharply over direct-mapped at modest cost.

Glossary

Set-associative cache
Cache with N slots per index, allowing any of N to hold a block from that index.
Set
Group of slots sharing the same index.
LRU (Least Recently Used)
Replacement policy evicting the slot that hasn't been used for the longest time.
Fully associative
Any block can go in any slot; no conflict misses.
Pseudo-LRU
Approximation of LRU using less hardware; standard in real caches.

Write-through = update cache AND memory now (simple, needs a write buffer). Write-back = update cache only, flush the dirty block on eviction (fast, needs a dirty bit). Pairing each with its cost is a standing exam question.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Cache misses are the cost in the AMAT formula. Knowing the categories — compulsory, capacity, conflict — and the techniques to reduce each is what cache-aware programmers and architects work on. Cache miss reduction is one of the highest-leverage performance optimizations.

Core concepts

1. Compulsory misses. First access to a block. Inevitable — the block hasn't been touched before, so it can't be in the cache. Sometimes called 'cold misses.' Reduced only by prefetching: the cache (or programmer) speculatively fetches blocks before they're needed.

2. Capacity misses. Working set exceeds cache size. Even a fully associative cache misses these — the data simply doesn't fit. Reduced by using smaller working sets (block algorithms, tiling) or larger caches.

3. Conflict misses. Set-associative cache misses caused by limited associativity, not capacity. The block is no longer in cache because something else mapped to the same set evicted it. Reduced by increasing associativity. Disappear in fully associative caches.

4. Reducing miss rate. Bigger cache: more blocks fit (capacity). Higher associativity: fewer conflicts. Bigger blocks: more spatial locality, fewer compulsory misses (within the block) — but cost: bigger blocks waste capacity if accesses are scattered. Each lever affects miss rate, hit time, and area differently.

5. Reducing miss penalty. Multi-level caches: L2 catches L1 misses much faster than memory. Critical-word-first delivery: the requested word arrives first; the rest of the block fills in after. Non-blocking caches: continue serving hits while a miss is pending. Each saves cycles on miss.

6. Reducing hit time. Small, simple caches hit faster. Way prediction: predict which way of a set holds the block; check that one first. Pipelining the cache. Critical for L1 because hit time is in the path of every load.

7. Real cache profiling. perf, cachegrind, Intel VTune. Show miss rates by code location and by cache level. Often the highest-impact optimization is realizing the miss rate on a hot loop is 30% and figuring out why. Profile before guessing.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Optimizing without measuring — cache behavior is hard to predict; miss rates surprise even experts.
  • Increasing associativity too much for L1 — slows hit time, often a net loss.
  • Choosing block size by tradition — modern hardware often benefits from larger blocks (128 bytes) due to better prefetching.
  • Treating all misses the same — compulsory, capacity, and conflict misses respond to different fixes.

Quick recap

Three miss types: compulsory (first access), capacity (working set too big), conflict (limited associativity). Reduce miss rate via bigger cache, higher associativity, larger blocks. Reduce miss penalty via multi-level caches, critical-word-first, non-blocking. Reduce hit time via small simple caches, way prediction. Profile real workloads; cache behavior is empirical.

Glossary

Compulsory miss
First-time access to a block; unavoidable without prefetching.
Capacity miss
Miss because the working set exceeds cache size.
Conflict miss
Miss in a set-associative cache because of limited associativity.
Critical-word-first
Cache fill optimization delivering the requested word before the rest of the block.
Non-blocking cache
Cache that continues to serve hits while a miss is being fetched.

AMAT — average memory access time: AMAT = hit_time + miss_rate × miss_penalty. Improve any of the three and memory gets faster; the formula also explains why tiny miss-rate changes matter when the penalty is huge.

📖 Worked example — a virtual address walks to a physical one

WORKED EXAMPLE — translate with 4 KB pages
Virtual address 0x00403204, page size 4 KB (12 offset bits):
• Virtual page number = 0x00403; offset = 0x204.
• TLB lookup of 0x00403: hit → physical frame (say 0x1A2) instantly.
• TLB miss → walk the page table in memory; valid entry → frame 0x1A2, refill TLB.
• Entry invalid → page fault: OS loads the page from disk (millions of cycles), updates the table, retries.
Physical address = frame ‖ offset = 0x1A2204. The offset NEVER changes — only the page number translates.
⚠️ TLB IS A CACHE OF TRANSLATIONS
Not data — translations. Hierarchy of pain: TLB hit (~free) → TLB miss/page-table walk (tens of cycles) → page fault (disk, astronomically slow, OS steps in). Rank those three and you answer half the VM questions.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Virtual memory gives each process its own private address space, isolates processes from each other, and lets the OS swap pages to disk. The TLB caches virtual-to-physical translations, making this fast on average. Both are essential to modern operating systems.

Core concepts

1. Virtual addresses vs physical. Programs use virtual addresses. The MMU (Memory Management Unit) translates each to a physical address before memory access. Each process has its own virtual address space; the OS maintains per-process page tables mapping virtual pages to physical frames.

2. Pages and frames. Page: a fixed-size chunk of virtual memory (typically 4 KB). Frame: a fixed-size chunk of physical memory. The page table maps virtual page numbers to physical frame numbers. Pages of one process can be in any frame, scattered, or absent (paged out to disk).

3. The page table. Per-process structure mapping virtual page numbers to physical frame numbers. With 32-bit virtual addresses and 4 KB pages, 1 million entries per process — too big for one flat table. Multi-level page tables (2, 3, or 4 levels) handle this by keeping unused parts unallocated.

4. Page faults. Access a virtual page that's not in physical memory (paged out, never loaded, or invalid). The MMU raises a page fault. The OS handles it: legitimate access — load from disk (slow); illegitimate (segfault) — kill the process. Real CPUs handle page faults dozens to thousands of times per second.

5. The TLB — Translation Lookaside Buffer. Hardware cache of recent page-table translations. 64 to 1024 entries typically. Each access: check TLB. Hit: get physical frame in 1 cycle. Miss: walk page table (3-5 memory accesses). TLB efficiency dominates large-memory workloads. TLB shootdown (invalidating entries on context switch or page table change) is its own performance concern.

6. Permission bits in page table entries. Each page-table entry has flags: present, readable, writable, executable, user-accessible, dirty (modified), accessed. The MMU enforces these. Read-only data, no-execute stacks, kernel/user separation are all enforced by these bits. Memory protection is hardware-mediated.

7. Why virtual memory enables so much. Process isolation (one process can't see another's memory). Demand paging (load only what's used). Swapping (extend memory beyond physical RAM). Shared memory (map same frame into multiple processes). Memory-mapped files (frames backed by file blocks). Copy-on-write fork (shared pages until first write). All built on the page-table mechanism.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Confusing virtual and physical addresses — different concepts; the MMU is the translator.
  • Underestimating TLB importance — random-access workloads on large data spend more time in TLB misses than in the actual computation.
  • Ignoring page size choice — modern CPUs support huge pages (2 MB, 1 GB) for large-memory apps; 4 KB pages cause TLB pressure.
  • Treating page faults as exceptional — they happen constantly in normal operation.

Quick recap

Virtual memory gives each process its own address space, mapped through page tables to physical frames. Page faults handle missing pages — load from disk or signal an error. The TLB caches translations, making most accesses fast. Permission bits in page-table entries enforce read-only, no-execute, and user/kernel separation. Process isolation, swapping, sharing, and copy-on-write all build on this mechanism.

Glossary

Virtual memory
Mechanism providing each process its own address space mapped through page tables.
Page / frame
Page is a virtual memory unit; frame is a physical memory unit (typically 4 KB).
Page table
Per-process structure mapping virtual pages to physical frames.
TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer)
Hardware cache of recent virtual-to-physical translations.
Page fault
Trap raised when accessing a virtual page not in physical memory.

📖 Worked example — disk access time, computed

WORKED EXAMPLE — total time for one 512-byte read
Drive: 4ms average seek, 15,000 RPM, 100 MB/s transfer.
• Seek = 4 ms (move the arm to the track).
• Rotational delay = half a spin = 0.5 × (60/15000) s = 2 ms.
• Transfer = 512 B / 100 MB/s ≈ 0.005 ms.
Total ≈ 6 ms — and virtually ALL of it is mechanical positioning, not data movement. That’s why random small reads murder spinning disks while sequential streaming is fine.
⚠️ AVERAGE ROTATION = HALF A REVOLUTION
The disk is equally likely to be anywhere in its spin, so the expected wait is half a rotation: 0.5 × 60/RPM. Forgetting the 0.5 (or using full rotation) is the standard lost point.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Hard disk drives still store the bulk of the world's data despite the rise of SSDs. The mechanics — spinning platters, moving heads, sectors — explain their performance characteristics: very fast sequential access, very slow random access. Knowing the mechanics is essential for storage decisions.

Core concepts

1. The physical structure. One or more magnetic platters spinning at 5400-15000 RPM. A read/write head floats nanometers above each surface. The head moves radially (seek). Data is stored as magnetic patterns on concentric tracks. Each track divided into sectors (typically 512 bytes or 4 KB).

2. Tracks, sectors, cylinders. Track: one circular path on a platter. Sector: a fixed-size segment of a track. Cylinder: all tracks at the same radial position across all platters (a stack you can read without moving the head). Modern drives use Zoned Bit Recording: outer tracks have more sectors than inner ones.

3. Seek time, rotational latency, transfer time. Seek time: head movement to the right track (3-15 ms typical). Rotational latency: wait for the right sector to rotate under the head (avg = half a rotation, so 4 ms at 7200 RPM). Transfer time: actually reading the data (sector / data rate). Total access time = seek + rotational + transfer.

4. Average access time calculation. Average seek (manufacturer spec, e.g., 8 ms) + half rotation (4 ms at 7200 RPM) + transfer for one sector (negligible). Total: ~12 ms per random access. Compared to memory's ~100 ns, that's 100,000x slower. Sequential reads are far faster — no seek between sectors.

5. Caching and read-ahead. HDDs have onboard caches (8-256 MB). Read-ahead caches sequential blocks proactively. Write caches absorb writes. The OS's page cache adds another layer. Cache hits hide some of the mechanical latency; cache misses still pay the full price.

6. HDD vs SSD characteristics. HDD: $0.02/GB, 100 IOPS random, 200 MB/s sequential. SSD: $0.10/GB, 10,000+ IOPS random, 3,000+ MB/s sequential. SSDs win on random access and IOPS by orders of magnitude; HDDs hold the cost edge for bulk capacity.

7. Why HDDs persist. Cheaper per byte for large capacities. Backups, archival storage, video libraries, cold data. Cloud providers use HDDs for object stores (S3 Glacier) and SSDs for hot tiers. The mix is workload-driven and economic, not technological alone.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Comparing HDDs and SSDs only on sequential bandwidth — random-access performance gap is enormous.
  • Designing a database without considering disk seek times — random reads kill performance.
  • Forgetting that drive caches can return stale data on power loss — fsync is needed for durability.
  • Treating IOPS specs as absolute — real workloads have access patterns that differ from benchmark.

Quick recap

HDDs use spinning magnetic platters and moving heads. Total access time = seek + rotational + transfer. Random access is ~12 ms; sequential is much faster. SSDs win on random and IOPS by orders of magnitude; HDDs win on cost per GB. Modern systems use a tiered mix: SSDs for hot, HDDs for cold. Caching and read-ahead hide some mechanical latency.

Glossary

Track / sector / cylinder
Spatial divisions of a magnetic disk: track is a circle, sector is a segment, cylinder is a stack of tracks.
Seek time
Time for the read/write head to move to the target track.
Rotational latency
Time waiting for the target sector to rotate under the head.
IOPS
Input/Output Operations Per Second; key random-access performance metric.
Zoned Bit Recording
Storage technique where outer tracks hold more sectors than inner tracks for better density.

📖 Worked example — why SSDs behave differently

WORKED EXAMPLE — the update that isn’t in-place
Flash rules: read a PAGE (~4 KB) fast, write only to ERASED pages, and erase only whole BLOCKS (~hundreds of pages).

So “overwrite 4 KB” actually means: write the new data to a FRESH page elsewhere, mark the old page stale, remap. Later, garbage collection copies a block’s live pages away and erases it. The FTL (flash translation layer) hides all this and also does wear leveling — spreading writes so no block hits its ~10⁵ erase-cycle limit early.
⚠️ NO SEEK ≠ NO QUIRKS
SSDs: no mechanical delay (random reads shine, ~100× disk), but limited write endurance and write amplification from GC. “Why do SSDs wear out?” → finite erase cycles per block; wear leveling is the mitigation.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

SSDs are the dominant storage for everything except bulk archival. The underlying flash memory has unique characteristics — fast reads, slow writes, finite write endurance, block-erase-then-program semantics — that shape SSD design. The flash translation layer (FTL) hides much of this from software.

Core concepts

1. NAND vs NOR flash. NAND: cheaper per bit, smaller cells, used for SSDs and large storage. Sequential read (good for files), block-erase-then-write. NOR: random-access read like RAM, fast, more expensive — used for boot ROMs and embedded code storage. NAND dominates SSDs.

2. The cell, page, block hierarchy. Cell: stores 1, 2, 3, or 4 bits (SLC, MLC, TLC, QLC). More bits per cell: cheaper, slower, less durable. Page: smallest read/write unit (4-16 KB typical). Block: smallest erase unit (256 KB - 4 MB). You can write a page once after erase; rewriting requires erasing the entire block.

3. The asymmetry: read fast, write slow, erase very slow. Read a page: ~50 µs. Program (write) a page: ~500 µs. Erase a block: ~2-5 ms. The orders-of-magnitude difference shapes SSD design. Random reads are fast; random writes require finding a free page or erasing a block first.

4. Wear leveling and endurance. Each cell can be programmed/erased only a limited number of times (1K-100K depending on type). The FTL distributes writes evenly across all blocks (wear leveling) so no single block wears out first. Cells slowly become less reliable; controllers retire bad blocks over the SSD's life.

5. The Flash Translation Layer (FTL). SSD firmware that maps logical block addresses (what the OS sees) to physical pages (where the data actually lives). Handles wear leveling, garbage collection, bad-block management. Hides the erase-before-write asymmetry: writes go to free pages; old pages marked invalid; garbage collection reclaims them in the background.

  • Filling an SSD to 100% — leaves no spare blocks for garbage collection; write performance crashes.

  • Choosing QLC for write-heavy workloads — more bits per cell means slower and less durable.

Quick recap

NAND flash is the basis of SSDs. Cells store multiple bits (SLC, MLC, TLC, QLC). Read-fast, write-slow, erase-very-slow asymmetry. The FTL handles wear leveling, garbage collection, bad blocks — translating logical addresses to physical pages. Write amplification means one logical write costs several physical ones. TRIM tells the SSD what's free, enabling efficient garbage collection. Sustained performance depends on free space.

Glossary

NAND flash
Type of flash memory used in SSDs; sequential-friendly, erase-block-organized.
FTL (Flash Translation Layer)
SSD firmware mapping logical blocks to physical pages; handles wear leveling and garbage collection.
Write amplification
Ratio of physical writes to logical writes; affects performance and wear.
Wear leveling
Distributing writes across cells to avoid premature failure of frequently-written ones.

OS-to-SSD command marking blocks as unused, enabling efficient garbage collection.

📖 Worked example — polling vs interrupts vs DMA

WORKED EXAMPLE — receive a network packet three ways
• Polling: CPU asks “done yet?” in a loop — simple, but burns cycles proportional to the wait.
• Interrupt: device taps the CPU when data arrives; CPU handles it then resumes — great for occasional events, but per-event overhead.
• DMA: CPU tells the DMA controller “move this buffer,” goes back to work, and gets ONE interrupt when the whole transfer finishes — the answer for bulk data.

Rule of thumb the exam wants: rare/small events → interrupts; constant tiny checks → polling can win; large blocks → DMA, always.
⚠️ DMA BYPASSES THE CPU, NOT MEMORY
DMA moves device↔memory without CPU copying — but it shares the memory bus (cycle stealing) and can make cached copies stale (the coherence problem that ch8 formalizes).
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

I/O — disk, network, peripherals — connects the CPU to the rest of the world. The I/O subsystem's design (buses, interrupts, DMA) determines whether the CPU spends most of its time computing or waiting. Modern systems have evolved from simple buses to high-throughput point-to-point interconnects.

Core concepts

1. Memory-mapped vs port-mapped I/O. Memory-mapped: device registers appear at specific memory addresses. CPU reads and writes them like memory. Standard on RISC ISAs (ARM, MIPS, RISC-V). Port-mapped: separate I/O instructions and address space. x86 still has it (in/out instructions) but mostly uses memory-mapped now. Memory-mapped is simpler and dominant.

2. Polling vs interrupts vs DMA. Polling: CPU repeatedly checks if device is ready. Wasteful when device is slow. Interrupts: device signals CPU when ready; CPU does other work meanwhile. Standard for slow-to-medium devices. DMA (Direct Memory Access): device transfers data directly to/from memory without CPU involvement; CPU is interrupted on completion. Standard for high-throughput devices.

3. The interrupt mechanism. Device asserts an interrupt line. CPU finishes current instruction, saves state, jumps to interrupt handler. Handler reads device status, copies data, dismisses interrupt. CPU resumes. Modern systems have hundreds of interrupts per second from disk, network, timers, USB.

4. DMA fundamentals. Device requests memory access from a DMA controller (now usually integrated into devices). DMA controller transfers data to/from memory while CPU does other work. CPU is notified on completion. Disk reads, network packets, audio playback all use DMA. Without it, CPU would copy every byte and waste enormous time.

5. PCIe — the modern interconnect. PCI Express. Point-to-point serial links between CPU and devices. Lanes (1x, 4x, 8x, 16x) provide scalable bandwidth — 1 GB/s per lane in PCIe 4.0. NVMe SSDs, GPUs, network cards all sit on PCIe. Replaced legacy PCI buses. Each generation roughly doubles bandwidth.

6. SATA, USB, Ethernet — peripheral standards. SATA: HDD/SSD interface (6 Gbps in SATA III). NVMe over PCIe is replacing it for SSDs. USB: universal peripheral standard (USB 3.x: 5+ Gbps; USB4: 40 Gbps). Ethernet: networking (1, 10, 25, 100 Gbps). Each standard has its niche; speed scaling continues.

7. I/O performance limits. CPU can issue I/O at billions of ops per second; storage and network are orders of magnitude slower. CPU often blocks waiting (idle time). Async I/O (epoll, io_uring) lets CPU continue working while I/O is in flight. The discipline is mostly about hiding I/O latency.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Polling fast devices — wastes CPU when interrupts would yield.
  • Polling slow devices when high IOPS — interrupt overhead exceeds gain; modern NVMe sometimes prefers polling.
  • Forgetting DMA — CPU copying packet data is far slower than DMA does it.
  • Building synchronous I/O paths in high-throughput servers — CPU sits idle; async I/O multiplies throughput.

Quick recap

I/O connects CPU to devices via memory-mapped (or port-mapped) addressing. Polling vs interrupts vs DMA represent three coordination strategies — DMA dominates for high-throughput. PCIe is the modern interconnect, replacing old buses with point-to-point serial links. SATA, USB, Ethernet have specific niches. I/O performance is mostly about hiding latency; async I/O is the modern technique.

Glossary

Memory-mapped I/O
Device registers appear at memory addresses; access via load/store.
DMA (Direct Memory Access)
Device transfers data to/from memory without CPU mediation.
Interrupt
Hardware signal causing CPU to suspend current work and run a handler.
PCIe
Point-to-point serial interconnect for modern peripherals; lanes scale bandwidth.
Async I/O
Programming model where I/O operations don't block the calling thread.

A bus is a shared communication pathway connecting components — CPU, memory, and devices exchange data over it. Shared means arbitration: only one talker at a time, which is why bus width and speed shape system throughput.

📖 Worked example — availability & RAID levels, computed

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — availability from MTTF/MTTR
A server has MTTF (mean time to failure) = 1,000 hours and MTTR (mean time to repair) = 10 hours.
Availability = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR) = 1000 / 1010 ≈ 99.0%.
Cut repair time to 1 hour: 1000/1001 ≈ 99.9% — an extra “nine” from faster repair alone. Dependability improves by failing less (MTTF↑) OR recovering faster (MTTR↓).
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — pick the RAID level, 4 disks of 1 TB
• RAID 0 (striping): 4 TB usable, fastest — but ANY disk dying loses everything. Performance only.
• RAID 1 (mirroring): 2 TB usable (every byte twice) — survives a disk failure, costliest capacity.
• RAID 5 (striping + distributed parity): 3 TB usable (one disk’s worth of parity) — survives ONE failure; a lost block is rebuilt by XOR-ing the survivors.
• RAID 6 (double parity): 2 TB usable here — survives TWO simultaneous failures.
“Max capacity + speed, no protection” → 0; “simple full redundancy” → 1; “capacity-efficient single-failure protection” → 5; “protect during long rebuilds” → 6.
⚠️ RAID IS NOT A BACKUP
RAID survives DISK failures; it happily replicates deletions, corruption, and ransomware to every disk instantly. The exam distinction: RAID = availability; backup = recovery from data loss.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Storage devices fail. RAID combines multiple drives into arrays that survive individual drive failures. Knowing the standard configurations — RAID 0, 1, 5, 6, 10 — and their tradeoffs is essential for system architecture and capacity planning.

Core concepts

1. MTTF, MTTR, availability. Mean Time To Failure: average time before a component fails. Mean Time To Repair: average time to recover after failure. Availability = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR). For 99.99% availability ('four nines'), an hour of downtime per year is the budget. RAID and redundancy improve availability by reducing recovery time and tolerating failures.

2. RAID 0 — striping for performance. Data split across two or more drives in stripes. Reads and writes go to multiple drives in parallel. Throughput increases linearly with drive count. NO redundancy: any drive failure loses all data. Good for non-critical, performance-driven workloads (scratch space, video editing).

3. RAID 1 — mirroring for redundancy. Two (or more) drives hold identical copies. Any drive can fail; data survives on the others. Read throughput can be doubled (split reads across copies). Write performance is the same as one drive. Capacity is half (with two-way mirror). Critical data, small to medium volumes.

4. RAID 5 — distributed parity. N drives. Each stripe of data has parity (XOR) on one drive, rotated across drives so no single drive holds all parity. Tolerates one drive failure. Capacity: (N-1)/N. Common for medium-sized arrays. Write performance suffers (parity must be recomputed). Rebuild after failure is slow and risky on large arrays.

5. RAID 6 — double parity. Like RAID 5 but with two independent parity blocks per stripe. Tolerates two simultaneous drive failures. Capacity: (N-2)/N. Standard for large arrays where rebuild times are long enough that a second failure during rebuild is plausible.

6. RAID 10 — striping plus mirroring. Combine RAID 1 (mirroring) with RAID 0 (striping). High performance and high redundancy. Capacity: N/2. Used for high-performance critical workloads (databases). More expensive but the best of both worlds.

7. RAID is not backup. RAID protects against drive failures. It does not protect against: corruption (a bug writes bad data; both copies are corrupt), deletion (rm -rf goes to all mirrors), ransomware (encryption applies to all drives), or disasters (the whole rack is gone). Backups — separate, ideally offline, ideally offsite — remain essential.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Treating RAID as backup — it isn't; many incidents need real backups.
  • Running RAID 5 on huge arrays — rebuild after a drive failure can take days; second failure during rebuild loses data.
  • Forgetting that RAID 0 has no redundancy — any failure loses everything.
  • Underestimating MTTR — fast hardware replacement means little if data restoration takes days.

Quick recap

MTTF and MTTR determine availability. RAID 0 stripes for performance, no redundancy. RAID 1 mirrors for redundancy. RAID 5 distributes parity, tolerating one failure. RAID 6 has two parity blocks, tolerating two failures. RAID 10 combines mirroring and striping. RAID is not backup; backups remain essential against corruption, deletion, and disaster. Choose RAID by workload's performance and durability needs.

Glossary

MTTF (Mean Time To Failure)
Average time before a component fails.
RAID 0 (striping)
Distributes data across drives for performance; no redundancy.
RAID 1 (mirroring)
Maintains identical copies on multiple drives for redundancy.
RAID 5
Distributed parity across N drives; tolerates one failure.
RAID 6
Double parity; tolerates two simultaneous failures.

📖 Worked example — Amdahl’s Law on a multicore

WORKED EXAMPLE — 8 cores, 95% parallel code
Speedup = 1 / ( (1 − 0.95) + 0.95/8 ) = 1 / (0.05 + 0.11875) = ≈ 5.9× — not 8×.

⚠️ SMP = SHARED MEMORY, ONE ADDRESS SPACE
A multicore/SMP machine has every core seeing the SAME memory — convenient, but it creates the coherence problem (next section). Clusters (separate memories, message passing) are the contrasting model.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

When frequency scaling stopped, multiple cores became the path forward. Symmetric multiprocessing (SMP) — multiple identical cores sharing memory — is the dominant architecture today. Knowing the parallelism types and Amdahl's Law explains both the opportunities and the limits.

Core concepts

1. Types of parallelism. ILP (Instruction-Level Parallelism): different instructions in the same thread overlap (pipelining, superscalar). DLP (Data-Level Parallelism): same operation on many data elements (SIMD, GPU). TLP (Thread-Level Parallelism): different threads run concurrently. RLP (Request-Level Parallelism): independent requests (web server). Each is exploited differently.

2. Symmetric multiprocessing (SMP). Multiple identical cores sharing one memory and one address space. Any core can run any thread; the OS schedules. Cache-coherent: cores see consistent values for shared memory. The dominant multicore architecture: every modern CPU is SMP.

3. Shared memory vs distributed memory. Shared memory: cores share one physical memory (SMP). Easy to program, doesn't scale beyond ~100 cores due to coherence cost. Distributed memory: each node has its own memory; communication via message passing (clusters, supercomputers). Scales to thousands of nodes; harder to program.

4. Amdahl's Law. Speedup = 1 / ((1 - P) + P/N) where P is the fraction of work that's parallelizable and N is the number of cores. With 95% parallel, max speedup at infinite cores is 20x. Even tiny serial portions cap parallel speedup. Reality of multicore: most code has serial sections that limit benefit.

5. Strong scaling vs weak scaling. Strong scaling: fixed problem size, more cores. Speedup limited by Amdahl's Law. Weak scaling: problem grows with cores; each core has the same work. Scales much further. Different goals: faster solution to fixed problem vs solving bigger problems.

6. The challenges of multicore programming. Race conditions: concurrent threads need synchronization. Deadlocks: threads waiting on each other. False sharing: independent data on the same cache line causes contention. Tuning parallelism is one of the harder skills in performance engineering.

7. Multicore in the wild. 4-16 cores in laptops and desktops. 32-64 in workstations. 100+ in servers. Specialized accelerators (GPUs, TPUs) have thousands of small cores. Heterogeneous systems combine: a few big cores for serial work, many small for parallel. Modern computing is multicore at every scale.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Expecting linear speedup from more cores — Amdahl's Law caps it.
  • Ignoring synchronization overhead — at high core counts, locks become bottlenecks.
  • Treating shared memory as scaling forever — past 64-128 cores, message passing or NUMA-aware programming wins.
  • Underestimating false sharing — 'independent' data on the same cache line bottlenecks performance.

Quick recap

Parallelism types: ILP (within thread), DLP (data parallel, SIMD), TLP (threads), RLP (independent requests). SMP is the dominant multicore architecture: cores share memory and an address space. Amdahl's Law limits parallel speedup based on serial fraction. Strong scaling vs weak scaling represent different goals. Multicore programming involves race conditions, deadlocks, and false sharing as new challenges.

Glossary

SMP (Symmetric Multiprocessor)
Architecture with multiple identical cores sharing one memory.
Amdahl's Law
Formula limiting parallel speedup based on the serial fraction of work.
TLP (Thread-Level Parallelism)
Multiple threads executing concurrently.
Strong scaling
Fixed problem size with more cores; limited by Amdahl's Law.
False sharing
Performance issue where independent variables on the same cache line cause unnecessary coherence traffic.
