📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — cache coherence with MSI/snooping

WORKED EXAMPLE — two cores, one variable
x = 5 in memory. Core A reads x (cached, Shared). Core B reads x (cached, Shared). Now A writes x = 7:
1. A broadcasts an invalidate on the bus; B’s copy → Invalid.
2. A’s copy → Modified (dirty, the one true value).
3. B later reads x → miss → A supplies 7 (or writes back first); both → Shared.

Every cache snoops the shared bus for such broadcasts. Guarantee: no core ever reads a stale value — writes to a location are seen in a consistent order.
⚠️ FALSE SHARING — COHERENCE’S TAX
Two cores updating DIFFERENT variables that share one cache line ping-pong the line back and forth (invalidate storms) — correct results, terrible speed. The fix is padding/aligning hot variables apart. Favorite “why is my parallel code slow?” answer.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

When multiple cores cache the same memory, they need to see consistent values. Cache coherence protocols (MESI, MOESI) maintain this. Memory consistency models define what behaviors programmers can assume. Both are crucial for correct multithreaded code on multicore CPUs.

Core concepts

1. The cache coherence problem. Core 1 and Core 2 both cache value X = 5. Core 1 writes X = 6. Without coherence, Core 2 still reads 5 from its cache. Different cores see different values for the same memory location — broken. Coherence protocols ensure all cores see the same write order.

2. MESI protocol — basic states. Each cache line has a state: Modified (this core's copy is the only valid one and has been changed), Exclusive (this core has the only copy, unchanged), Shared (multiple cores have copies, all unchanged), Invalid (this copy is stale). Transitions on reads, writes, and snoops maintain coherence.

3. Snooping caches. Each core's cache watches the bus (or interconnect) for transactions affecting cached lines. When another core writes a line this cache holds, this cache invalidates its copy. Cheap for small core counts; doesn't scale past ~8-16 cores due to bus traffic.

4. Directory-based coherence. Centralized (or distributed) directory tracks which cores have copies of each cache line. On write, invalidate only those cores. Scales better than snooping. Used in larger systems and across multiple sockets. More complex to implement.

5. Write-invalidate vs write-update. Write-invalidate: writer invalidates other cores' copies; they fetch on next access. Standard. Write-update: writer broadcasts the new value to other caches. Higher bandwidth; only useful when many cores are reading the same value. Most modern systems use write-invalidate.

6. Memory consistency models. Coherence is per-location. Consistency is across locations. Sequential consistency: as if one core executed all instructions in some interleaved order. Hard to implement; slow. Relaxed models (TSO on x86, weaker on ARM): allow some reorderings for performance. Programmers use memory barriers to enforce ordering when needed.

7. What this means for programmers. Naive shared-memory code 'works' most of the time but has subtle bugs from reordering and visibility. Use synchronization primitives (locks, atomics, barriers) instead of relying on raw reads and writes. Modern languages provide memory models (Java's, C++'s std::atomic) that abstract over hardware variation.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Ignoring memory consistency — naive multithreaded code 'works' until reordering surfaces a race.
  • Adding volatile (in C/C++) and assuming it provides synchronization — it doesn't.
  • Forgetting that x86 is TSO and ARM is weaker — code that 'works on x86' may break on ARM.
  • Designing systems with frequent shared writes — coherence traffic dominates and bottlenecks scaling.

Quick recap

Cache coherence ensures all cores see the same writes to the same location. MESI states (Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid) and snooping or directory protocols maintain it. Write-invalidate dominates. Memory consistency defines ordering across locations. Sequential consistency is intuitive but slow; relaxed models (TSO, weaker) are common. Programmers should use synchronization primitives, not rely on raw memory accesses for ordering.

Glossary

Cache coherence
Property that all cores see consistent values for shared memory locations.
MESI
Cache coherence protocol with Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid line states.
Snooping cache
Cache that watches the interconnect for transactions affecting its cached lines.
Memory consistency model
Rules defining the orderings of memory operations programmers can assume.
Memory barrier
Instruction enforcing ordering of memory operations across reorderings.

📖 Worked example — SIMD: one instruction, many data

WORKED EXAMPLE — add two arrays with vector registers
Scalar loop: 4 loads, 4 adds, 4 stores per 4 elements. With 128-bit SIMD registers (4 × 32-bit lanes):
vld  v1, a[i..i+3]     # load FOUR elements at once
vld  v2, b[i..i+3]
vadd v3, v1, v2        # four additions in ONE instruction
vst  v3, c[i..i+3]
One instruction does the work of four — data-level parallelism. This is Flynn’s SIMD (single instruction, multiple data); a normal core is SISD; a multicore running different threads is MIMD. GPUs push SIMD to thousands of lanes.
⚠️ SIMD LOVES REGULAR DATA
Vectorization needs same-operation-on-contiguous-elements (arrays, images, matrices). Branchy, pointer-chasing code doesn’t vectorize — “which workload benefits from SIMD?” → the regular, data-parallel one, every time.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Single Instruction, Multiple Data (SIMD) processes multiple data elements in parallel with one instruction. It's how modern CPUs vectorize numerical and multimedia code, and it's the architectural foundation of GPUs. For data-parallel workloads, SIMD speedups are dramatic.

Core concepts

1. The SIMD idea. One instruction operates on multiple data elements simultaneously. Add four 32-bit integers in parallel with one ALU operation. Special wide registers hold the data (128, 256, or 512 bits). Different from threads: same instruction, multiple data; not multiple instruction streams.

2. x86 SIMD evolution. MMX (1996, 64-bit). SSE (1999, 128-bit). SSE2-4 added more operations. AVX (2011, 256-bit). AVX-512 (2013-, 512-bit). Each extension adds wider registers and more operations. Modern x86 CPUs have all of these; software picks based on what's available.

3. ARM NEON and SVE. ARM's SIMD: NEON (128-bit, used since ARMv7). SVE (Scalable Vector Extension, modern ARM): variable-width vectors (128 to 2048 bits). Code targets a logical width that runs efficiently regardless of physical width. Apple Silicon's vector unit uses NEON.

4. Compiler auto-vectorization. Modern compilers detect parallelizable loops and emit SIMD code automatically. Loop bodies that are independent across iterations are candidates. Pragmas (#pragma omp simd) hint the compiler. Often gives 2-8x speedup transparent to the programmer.

5. Manual SIMD via intrinsics. When auto-vectorization fails, write SIMD explicitly: _mm_add_ps (SSE), _mm256_add_ps (AVX). Compiler intrinsics that map to SIMD instructions. More control, more effort. Used in performance-critical libraries (BLAS, image processing, video codecs).

6. Data-level parallelism vs thread-level. DLP: same operation on multiple values, one thread. TLP: different operations across threads. They compose: a thread can execute SIMD instructions, and many threads can each be running SIMD. Modern parallel code combines both.

7. GPUs as massive SIMD. GPUs have thousands of cores grouped into 'warps' or 'wavefronts' that execute in lockstep — many SIMD lanes. Originally for graphics; CUDA and OpenCL exposed them for general compute. Modern training of AI models leans heavily on GPU SIMD-style parallelism.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Writing SIMD code without measuring — alignment and pattern issues can make 'optimized' code slower.
  • Assuming auto-vectorization always works — small code changes can disable it; check the compiler output.
  • Ignoring SIMD — leaving 4-16x performance on the table for numerical loops.
  • Treating GPU programming as 'just SIMD' — memory coalescing, divergence, and shared memory are essential too.

Quick recap

SIMD: one instruction, many data elements. x86 has SSE through AVX-512; ARM has NEON and SVE; both vectorize numerical work. Compilers auto-vectorize many loops; intrinsics enable manual control. Data-level parallelism complements thread-level. GPUs scale SIMD to thousands of cores. Modern numerical and multimedia code lives or dies on SIMD utilization.

Glossary

SIMD
Single Instruction, Multiple Data — one instruction operates on multiple data elements.
AVX / AVX-512
x86 SIMD extensions with 256-bit and 512-bit wide registers.
NEON
ARM's SIMD extension with 128-bit registers.
Auto-vectorization
Compiler optimization that emits SIMD instructions for parallelizable loops.
Compiler intrinsics
Functions that map directly to SIMD instructions, giving manual control.
📊 FIGURE — the trend is specialisation
🎯 EXAM TIP
The direction of travel is heterogeneous computing — CPU plus GPU plus specialised accelerators — with more cores and domain-specific architectures. The driver is that general-purpose single-thread performance stopped improving, so gains now come from parallelism and from silicon designed for one kind of work.

Digital logic: gates, flip-flops & sequential circuits

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Every processor is built from tiny switches — logic gates — wired together. Gates that only depend on current inputs are combinational; add memory (state that persists) and you get sequential circuits, which is how hardware remembers bits.

THE BASIC GATES
GateOutput is 1 when…
ANDALL inputs are 1
ORANY input is 1
NOT (inverter)the single input is 0
NANDNOT all inputs are 1 (AND then invert)
NORall inputs are 0 (OR then invert)
XORthe inputs differ (odd number of 1s)

NAND and NOR are universal — any circuit can be built from NAND gates alone (or NOR alone).

COMBINATIONAL vs SEQUENTIAL
Combinational: output depends only on current inputs (adders, multiplexers, decoders — no memory). Sequential: output depends on current inputs AND stored state (flip-flops, registers, counters — has memory, driven by a clock).
⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

A latch stores one bit and is level-triggered (responds while the enable is high). A flip-flop is edge-triggered — it captures its input only on a clock edge (rising/falling), which keeps a whole chip in step. A D flip-flop stores the value of D at each clock edge. A register is just a row of flip-flops holding a multi-bit value; the CPU's register file is built from these.

📝 EXAM WORDING

Combinational = no memory, output = f(inputs now). Sequential = has memory + a clock. Latch = level-triggered; flip-flop = edge-triggered. NAND/NOR are universal gates. XOR = 1 when inputs differ.

🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
Which circuit type has memory and is driven by a clock?
  1. Combinational
  2. Sequential
  3. A single AND gate
  4. A multiplexer
Show answer
B. Sequential circuits (flip-flops, registers, counters) store state and update on a clock edge; combinational logic has no memory.

📖 Worked example — a hard performance/pipeline problem

WORKED EXAMPLE — effective CPI with stalls
A 5-stage pipeline runs at base CPI 1. The program: 20% loads with half causing a 1-cycle load-use stall; 15% branches with 20% mispredicted at 3-cycle penalty.

Stall CPI = (0.20 × 0.5 × 1) + (0.15 × 0.20 × 3) = 0.10 + 0.09 = 0.19.
Effective CPI = 1 + 0.19 = 1.19.
At 2 GHz, 10⁹ instructions take (10⁹ × 1.19) / (2×10⁹) = 0.595 s.

Recipe: base CPI + Σ(frequency × probability × penalty) for each stall source, then into the CPU-time equation. Every hard performance question is this template with different numbers.

Number Representation

Two's complement (n bits) represents values from -2^(n-1) to 2^(n-1)-1. To negate: invert all bits and add 1. The MSB carries weight -2^(n-1). Sign-extension replicates the MSB into new high bits.

IEEE-754 single (32-bit) = 1 sign, 8 exponent (bias 127), 23 fraction. Value = (-1)^s x 1.f x 2^(E-127) for normalized numbers. Steps: write magnitude in binary, normalize to 1.xxx x 2^e, exponent field = e+127, fraction = bits after the point.

KEY RESULTS
  • -6.25 = 0xC0C80000; 0x42480000 = 50.0; 0xC1200000 = -10.0
  • 0.1 has no exact single-precision form (0x3DCCCCCD).

Performance

FORMULAS
  • CPU time = Instrs x CPI / ClockRate = Instrs x CPI x CycleTime
  • Avg CPI = Sum(freq_i x CPI_i)
  • MIPS = ClockRate / (CPI x 10^6)
  • Amdahl: Speedup = 1 / ((1-f) + f/s); max = 1/(1-f)

Pipelining

An ideal k-stage pipeline runs N instructions in N+k-1 cycles. Hazards: structural (resource conflict), data (RAW), control (branches). Forwarding routes results from EX/MEM back to EX, removing most data stalls; a load-use hazard still costs one stall because data arrives only after MEM.

TECHNIQUE

Pipeline CPI = 1 + stall cycles per instruction. Multiply hazard frequency by penalty, sum, add to the base CPI of 1.

SUBTLETY

Amdahl caps speedup by the un-accelerated fraction; and MIPS is misleading across different ISAs because it ignores work per instruction.

📖 Worked example — a hard cache problem, start to finish

WORKED EXAMPLE — AMAT with two levels
L1: 1-cycle hit, 5% miss. L2: 10-cycle hit, 20% (local) miss. Memory: 100 cycles.

AMAT = L1 hit + L1 miss rate × (L2 hit + L2 miss rate × memory)
= 1 + 0.05 × (10 + 0.20 × 100)
= 1 + 0.05 × 30 = 2.5 cycles.

Without L2: 1 + 0.05 × 100 = 6 cycles — the L2 more than halved average access time. Work outside-in, and remember L2’s miss rate is LOCAL (of the requests that reach it), not global.

Cache Address Breakdown

Split the physical address into tag | index | block-offset. Offset = log2(block bytes). Number of sets = cache size / (block size x associativity); index = log2(sets). Tag = remaining high bits. Direct-mapped is 1-way; fully associative has 0 index bits (1 set).

FORMULAS
  • sets = C / (B x A), index bits = log2(sets)
  • tag bits = addr - index - offset
  • AMAT = HitTime + MissRate x MissPenalty
  • Two-level AMAT = Hit_L1 + MR_L1 x (Hit_L2 + MR_L2 x Pen_mem)
KEY RESULTS
  • 4-way 32KB, 64B blocks, 32-bit addr: offset 6, index 7, tag 19.
  • Two-level AMAT (Hit1, MR 4%, L2 hit10, L2 local MR 25%, mem 200) = 3.4 cycles.

Virtual Memory

VA splits into VPN | page offset, offset = log2(page size). A single-level page table has 2^VPN entries. The TLB caches recent VPN-to-PPN translations; a TLB miss walks the page table, a page fault fetches from disk.

TECHNIQUE

Local miss rate is relative to accesses reaching that level; global miss rate = product of local rates from L1 down. Use global rates when weighting by total references.

RAID

RAID-0 stripes (no redundancy). RAID-1 mirrors (usable = half). RAID-5 uses one distributed parity block (usable = N-1, survives 1 failure). RAID-6 adds a second parity (usable = N-2, survives 2).

SUBTLETY

A lower local L2 miss rate can still mean many memory accesses if L1 misses often - always convert to global rate before comparing designs.

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
THE 3-STEP LOOP
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
Start the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.

⚠ MOORE S LAW IS ABOUT TRANSISTORS, NOT SPEED The classic statement: transistor counts per chip double roughly every ~2 years. Clock speeds stopped scaling with them (the power wall) — which is exactly why the industry…

Performance Measurement

⚠ MHz/GHz ALONE NEVER DECIDES A 3 GHz CPU with CPI 4 is slower than a 2 GHz CPU with CPI 1 on the same instruction count. And Amdahl s Law caps any speedup by the fraction you DIDN T improve: speeding up 80% of a program by 10× still leaves the untouched 20%, capping overall speedup at 1/(0.2 + 0.8/10) ≈ 3.6×.

⚠ MUXES ARE THE ANSWER TO HOW DOES IT CHOOSE? Whenever two sources could feed one input (ALU s second operand: register or immediate? PC s next value: +4 or branch target?), a multiplexer selects — steered by control…

Control Unit & Instruction Cycle

⚠ DATAPATH MOVES, CONTROL DECIDES Exam phrasing: the datapath is the muscle (ALU, registers, memories, muxes); the control unit is the brain that sets the mux/write signals per instruction. Keep the two vocabularies…

⚠ BLOCKS EXIST BECAUSE OF SPATIAL LOCALITY Caches move multi-word BLOCKS, not single bytes, betting neighbors get used. Stride-through-memory access patterns (column-major walks of a row-major array) break the bet —…

Cache Basics: Direct-Mapped

⚠ TWO ADDRESSES, ONE SLOT = THRASHING Addresses 0x34 and 0xB4 can share index 3 with different tags — alternate between them and every access misses (conflict misses), even with the rest of the cache empty. That…

Set-Associative Caches & Replacement

⚠ MORE WAYS ≠ FREE Doubling associativity cuts conflict misses but adds comparators and can slow the hit path. Why not fully associative everywhere? → cost and hit time. Typical real answer: 4-8 way L1.

Cache Misses & Performance

⚠ WRITE POLICY VOCAB Write-through = update cache AND memory now (simple, needs a write buffer). Write-back = update cache only, flush the dirty block on eviction (fast, needs a dirty bit). Pairing each with its cost…

Virtual Memory & TLB

⚠ TLB IS A CACHE OF TRANSLATIONS Not data — translations. Hierarchy of pain: TLB hit (~free) → TLB miss/page-table walk (tens of cycles) → page fault (disk, astronomically slow, OS steps in). Rank those three and you can answer most TLB questions — the miss-penalty hierarchy is the point, not exact cycle counts.

"}, "C952/cheat/c8": {"body": "

⚠ AVERAGE ROTATION = HALF A REVOLUTION The disk is equally likely to be anywhere in its spin, so the expected wait is half a rotation: 0.5 × 60/RPM. Forgetting the 0.5 (or using full rotation) is the standard lost…

Flash Memory and SSDs

⚠ NO SEEK ≠ NO QUIRKS SSDs: no mechanical delay (random reads shine, ~100× disk), but limited write endurance and write amplification from GC. Why do SSDs wear out? → finite erase cycles per block; wear leveling is the…

I/O Subsystem & Buses

⚠ DMA BYPASSES THE CPU, NOT MEMORY DMA moves device↔memory without CPU copying — but it shares the memory bus (cycle stealing) and can make cached copies stale (the coherence problem that ch8 formalizes).

Dependability and RAID

⚠ RAID IS NOT A BACKUP RAID survives DISK failures; it happily replicates deletions, corruption, and ransomware to every disk instantly. The exam distinction: RAID = availability; backup = recovery from data loss.
